paragraph.text_eng: My late grandmother used to tell me all sorts of things. She told me about what happened a long time ago. She said that it must have been over there at what's called Niingidawitigweyaang ‘River Fork’ (Crow Wing)on the Mississippi where they got all kinds of food. They must have been fed with all sorts of things over there.

sentence.sent_text: Nookomisiban iko anooj gegoo ingii-ig.
Ingii-waawiindamaag gaa-izhiwebak mewinzha.
Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod iwidi iidog ayi'ing niingidawitigweyaang ogii-izhi-wiindaanaawaa iwidi gichi-ziibiing -- gaa-ondinamowaad iko anooj gegoo wiisiniwin.
Anooj gegoo gii-ashamaawag iidog iwidi.

paragraph.text_eng: Once some Indians -- I don’t know how many canoes of them there were -- -went there to fetch rations; they were given all sorts of things, blankets too. That’s where they must have been going. There was one elderly old man. It was there at -- -I don’t know what it’s called, indeed I have forgotten what that lake is called. There are seven little islands there. One of the little islands is really nice. There is a clearing there. They must have slept there on the way. Well, they're afraid that they would see the Sioux someplace. They slept there on their way.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ingoding anishinaabeg -- amanj gaa-tasoonagiziwaagwen -- mii iwidi ezhaawaad o-naadashamigoowinewaad; anooj gegoo gii-miinindwaa, waabooyaanan igaye.
Miish iidog iwidi ezhaawaad.
Miish giiwenh bezhig akiwenzii, gikaa.
Miish imaa i'iw -- gaawiin ingikendanziin ezhinikaadeg, aanawi go ingii-wandendaan ezhinikaadeg i'iw zaaga'igan.
Niizhwaachinoon imaa iniw minisensan.
Bezhig giiwenh minisens enda-onizhishin.
Bapashkwaa.
Mii iidog imaa gii-ani-nibaawaad.
Aaniish naa ogosaawaan igaye bwaanan iidog, ingoji ji-waabamaawaad.
Mii imaa gii-ani-nibaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: The old man says: “Leave me here,” that’s what the old man says. “Leave me here. I’ll be right here when you come back. Look for me here as you come by,” says the old man. There was only tobacco and his pipe. That old man was elderly.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ekidod a'aw akiwenzii: "Mii omaa nagazhishig," ikido giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii.
"Mii omaa nagazhishig, omaa.
Mii omaa ji-ayaayaan, bi-washki-giiweyeg apii.
Bimi-nandawaabamishiikeg," ikido giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii.
Mii eta go asemaan, odoopwaaganan.
Gichi-aya'aawi a'aw akiwenzii.

paragraph.text_eng: The old man stayed there and the Indians took off again. They went over there -- they call it Zhimaaganishii-oodenawens ‘Little Soldiertown’ -- -they were going after food. They must have been over there for a few days, maybe two or three, then they came back again. “Let’s go and look for our grandfather,” they say. So they landed their canoes there again.

sentence.sent_text: Miish sa giiwenh imaa gii-ayaad, gaa-izhi-maajaawaad miinawaa, gaa-izhi-maajaawaad ingiw anishinaabeg.
Miish iwidi gaa-izhaawaad -- zhimaaganishii-oodenawens ogii-idaanaawaa -- gii-naadiwaad i'iw wiisiniwin.
Maagizhaa iwidi noomag igo dasogon gaa-o-ayaawaagwen, maagizhaa gaye niizhogon, maagizhaa gaye nisogon, gaa-pi-izhi-maajaawaad miinawaa.
"Da naa, ani-waabamaadaa gimishoomisinaan," ikidowag giiwenh.
Mii imaa gaa-izhi-agwaa'owaad miinawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Although they went all around there, there was no old man there. He wasn’t there, there was nothing there. There wasn’t even a misko-waabowayaan ‘red blanket’; that’s what the ones they wore used to be called. There wasn’t anything there. They didn’t know what might have happened to him. There was just a gun there, an old gun, which they left behind. Well, they wouldn’t take it along.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa gaawiin awiiya iniw akiwenziiyan, miziwe imaa aano-gii-pabaa-izhaawaad.
Mii sa go gaawiin awiiya.
Gaawiin gegoo misko-waabowayaan; gii-izhi-wiindewan iko gaa-agwazhewaajin.
Mii gaye gaawiin gegoo i'iw.
Miish iidog amanj gaa-izhiwebizigwen.
Mii eta go baashkizigan eteg, gichi-gete-baashkiziganish, gaa-izhi-nagadamowaad.
Aaniish naa gaawiin odaa-mamoosiinaawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Although they kept going over there, they never saw the old man. They wondered where he was. Might not the Sioux have taken him? There was nothing. That old man was lost.

sentence.sent_text: Apane imaa aano-izhaawaad, mii gaawiin wiikaa ogii-waabamaasiwaawaan.
Mii dibi a'aw akiwenzii.
Gaawiin gaye bwaanan odaa-gii-mamigosiin.
Gaawiin sa go gegoo.
Mii sa go gii-wani'ind a'aw akiwenzii.

paragraph.text_eng: I was working here at the trading post. Just a little while ago, maybe it’s about two years ago. We are friends with one of the white people from Garrison, a storekeeper, and that woman came over. She says, “You used to hear what Perry Borden told about the old man who got left behind long ago,” she says to me. She’s talking English.

sentence.sent_text: Miish omaa, ingii-anokii omaa adaawewigamigong.
Noomaya go ingoji go niizho-biboonagadodog.
Bezhig imaa gichi-mookomaan iko ninagadenimaanaan mazhii'iganing, adaawewinini, gaa-pi-izhi-izhaad a'aw ikwe.
Miish i'iw ekidod a'aw: "Gigii-noondaan iko Perry Borden gaa-dibaajimod a'aw akiwenzii gaa-naganaawindibanen imaa mewinzha," indig.
Zhaaganaashiimo.

paragraph.text_eng: “Yes,” I tell her. “My grandmother used to tell me about it,” I tell her.

sentence.sent_text: "Eyan'," indinaa.
"Nookomis iko ingii-wiindamaag," indinaa.

paragraph.text_eng: “The boys found an old gun over there where they went to sleep,” she says. “Under the ground -- - I don’t know what they were doing under the ground -- - and that gun the boys found is still in pretty good shape.”

sentence.sent_text: "Ogii-mikaanaawaa ingiw gwiiwizensag imaa o-nibaawaad gichi-gete-baashkizigan," ikido.
"Anaamakamig igo imaa -- amanj iidog gaa-izhichigewaagwen imaa anaamakamig igo -- gegaa geyaabi onizhishin giiwenh baashkizigan, gii-mikamowaad ingiw gwiiwizensag."

paragraph.text_eng: Maybe it really happened the way it was told.

sentence.sent_text: Maagizhaa gaye, mii i'iw geget igo aayaawanogwen gaa-inaajimong.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go i'iw.

chapter.eng_title: When My Grandmother Heard About the War

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago it was my late grandmother who told me of the place called Aitkin; in Indian it’s called Bepashkojiishkiwagaag ‘Mudflats’. There was a town there. That’s where they always go shopping to buy things when they have money.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha nookomisiban igaye gii-tibaajimod, mii iwidi ezhi-wiindeg Aitkin; anishinaabewinikaade go bepashkojiishkiwagaag izhi-wiindemagad.
Oodena iidog imaa gii-tagon.
Mii iidog imaa apane ezhaawaad maa'ishkamowaad gegoo go adaawewaad ozhooniyaamiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: My late grandmother was acquainted with lots of white people there. She used to name them. But I have forgotten their names.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog a'aw nookomisiban niibowa ogii-nagadenimaawaan iniw gichi-mookomaanan imaa.
Ogii-waawiinaan iko ezhinikaazonid.
Ingii-wanendam-sh ezhinikaazowaad mii ingiw.

paragraph.text_eng: Once one of them came running out. He’s trembling. “Have you heard what’s happening? There’s a war. The Indians are taking captives at Leech Lake. Many in town are going to run away,” he must have said. “The white people are scared that they might be killed. They’re really scared. I don’t know what might be done to you people. Maybe you'll be taken prisoner, “that white man says.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding igo giiwenh bi-zaagizibatoowan.
Mii go giiwenh ezhi-baapagibinigonid.
"Ginoondaam ina ezhiwebak?
Miigaadim.
Anishinaabeg nawadiniwewag gaa-zagaskwaajimekaag.
Niibowa wii-ozhimowag imaa," ikidowidog, "mii imaa oodenaang.
Zegiziwag ingiw gichi-mookomaanag, aaniish naa mii akina ji-nisindwaa.
Enda-zegiziwag, Amanj iidog ge-izhi'igoowegwen.
Maagizhaa gaye ga-debibinigoom," ikido giiwenh a'aw gichi-mookomaan.

paragraph.text_eng: They must have understood him and they too got scared. Well, they leave some people behind; my mother, who was a young lady, must have been left behind too. They snuck away to come home.

sentence.sent_text: Maagizhaa gaye gaa-nisidotawaawaagwen, enda-zegiziwaad gaye wiinawaa.
Aaniish naa onaganaawaan imaa, mii iidog gaye nimaamaayan igo gii-oshkiniigikwewinid naganaawaad.
Mii iidog giimooj gaa-pi-izhi-maajaawaad gii-pi-giiwewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: At Neyaashiing (Vineland)the young men are in a state of excitement and are catching their horses. They want to ride to where the action is and go and help the Indians in the war.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog imaa neyaashiing imaa enda-baapinakamigiziwag giiwenh inigiw oshki-ininiwag debibinaawaad iniw odayiwaan.
Mii iwidi waa-apa'igowaad iwidi endanakandenig wii-o-naadamawaawaad iniw anishinaaben miigaanimind.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady used to tell.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.

paragraph.text_eng: More of what my grandmother told me. “What happened long ago,” she says.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa nookomis gaa-inaajimotawid.
"Mewinzha gaa-izhiwebak," ikido.

paragraph.text_eng: The Indians must be moving, perhaps to the point, to boil sap. I don’t know which way they must have gone. Maybe they move to Iskigamiziganing ‘Sap Boiling Place’. There’s a stream flowing there halfway, and the Indians are packing up in the morning to leave for over here so they can finish making the wigwams to stay in before it gets dark.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog imaa, maagizhaa gaye imaa neyaashiing, ingiw anishinaabeg goziwaad wii-iskigamizigewaad.
Dibi-sh akeyaa gaa-izhaawaagwen Maagizhaa gaye imaa iskigamiziganing izhi-goziwag.
Ziibiins idash imaa bimitigweyaa imaa aabita, ozhiwanikewaad ingiw anishinaabeg, bi-maajaawaad gigizheb ji-de-giizhiitaawaad, jibwaa-dibikadinig ji-ozhitoowaad iniw wiigiwaaman ji-ayaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: A while later a girl turns up missing along with her pack. She was sort of grown up. She disappeared, so one of the women went back to see what was happening to her because she might have fallen in the stream. The girl’s bundle was sitting there. Although she calls for her, she gets no reply from her. She goes around the area, but in vain. She can’t find her, so she turned back and went to tell of finding that little pack. “She’s not there anywhere.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go gomaapii go giiwenh, weniban giiwenh a'aw ikwezens, obimiwanaanens gaye wiin.
Gomaa go gii-inigini a'aw ikwezens.
Weniban giiwenh a'aw ikwezens, gaa-izhi-washki-giiwed giiwenh bezhig a'aw ikwe, nandawaabamaad aaniin ezhichigenid ji-gii-poozibizonid imaa ziibiinsing.
Gii-ateni giiwenh obimiwanaanens, mii a'aw ikwezens.
Aano-baabiibaagimaad, mii gaawiin onakomigosiin.
Miinawaa ko giiwenh ingoji aano-izhaa imaa.
Mii sa gaawiin omikawaasiin, gaa-izhi-washki-giiwed iidog gii-o-dibaajimod gii-mikang i'iw bimiwanaanens.
"Gaawiin imaa ingoji ayaasiin."

paragraph.text_eng: The Indians are scared about where the little girl has gone, she’s lost. There must have been some old men there, Indian doctors, perhaps conjurors. They give an old man tobacco and things -- - it’s getting late in the evening -- - so he would find out where she has gone. After a while, as the sun was setting, the girl walked in. She didn’t tell anything. They say everything to her (to get her to tell), but to no avail. She doesn’t tell where she had gone or what she had done.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa azhigwa zegiziwaad ingiw anishinaabeg aandi gaa-izhaad a'aw ikwezens, wanishing.
Miinawaa akiwenziiyag-sh iidog imaa gii-ayaawag, nenaandawii'iwejig, maagizhaa gaye jaasakiijig.
Mii azhigwa miinaawaad asemaan miinawaa anooj igo gegoo -- azhigwa ani-onaagoshininig -- - azhigwa ji-gikendang a'aw akiwenzii aandi gaa-izhaanid.
Mii go giiwenh azhigwa ani-bangishimog azhigwa, ani-bangishimog azhigwa, baanimaa go giiwenh gaa-piidaasamosed, mii a'aw ikwezens.
Mii go giiwenh gaawiin dibaajimosiin.
Miinawaa ko gegoo odaano-inaawaan.
Mii gaawiin dibaajimosiin aandi gaa-izhaad, aaniin gaa-izhichiged.

paragraph.text_eng: They keep asking the girl, it might be her older sisters or her aunts or her girl cousins: “Where did you go? Why don’t you tell where you went?”

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding-sh iidog igo apane gagwejimaawaad ingiw, maagizhaa gaye omisenyan, maagizhaa gaye onoshenyan a'aw ikwezens, maagizhaa gaye odaangoshenyan: "Aandi gaa-izhaayan?
Aaniin dadibaajimosiwan aandi gaa-izhaayan?"

paragraph.text_eng: After a while the girl gets sort of tired of this, so she told about it: “A man caught up to me there and took me. He put me on his shoulders and we went all around Mille Lacs Lake. Just when it was about sundown, he put me back where he got me. ‘Don’t ever tell!’ he told me,” the girl says. That’s what she said.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding sa iidog igo enda-ishkendam a'aw ikwezens, gaa-izhi-dibaajimod: "Inini imaa ingii-adimig, gaa-izhi-maajiizhid.
Imaa odinimaanganaang ingii-asig, gaa-izhi-giiwitaashkaayaang i'iw misi-zaaga'igan.
Miish miinawaa imaa azhigwa bangishimog gegaa, mii imaa gii-pagidinid gaa-ondinid.
'Gego wiikaa dibaajimoken,' ingii-ig," ikido giiwenh a'aw ikwezens.
Mii iidog i'iw gaa-ikidod.

paragraph.text_eng: So, sure enough, that girl died just a little while later. He had told her: “Don’t tell! You'll live long if you don’t tell.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo geget gaa-izhi-nibod wayiiba, mii a'aw ikwezens.
Ogii-igoon giiwenh: "Gego dibaajimoken.
Ginwenzh ga-bimaadiz dibaajimosiwan."

chapter.eng_title: When Aazhawakiwenzhiinh Almost Became A Windigo

paragraph.text_eng: More of long ago, how my namesake-old man, the one called Aazhawakiwenzhiinh, almost became a windigo. Someone working on a rabbit accidentally cut herself. He must have tasted the blood. That’s what he said. He recovered because they gave him boiling hot wild rice broth to drink; he was all right then. That’s all I know of that.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gichi-mewinzha, nii'awen'enh-kiwenzhiinh ko a'aw Aazhawakiwenzhiinh gaa-inind, gaa-izhi-wiindigoowid gegaa.
Awiiya iidog waaboozoon dazhiikawaad, gii-pitikonidizo.
Miish iidog maagizhaa gaye gaa-taangandamogwen i'iw miskwi.
Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod.
Miish gaa-onji-aabaakawizid niibowa manoominaaboo gichi-gizhaagamidenig gaa-izhi-mina'aawaad, ingoding igo gaa-izhi-aabaakawizid.
Miish eta minik gekendamaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Once I asked my grandmother: “Why do the Indians act like they want to become windigos, why do they become windigos? It is said that long ago they ate each other.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish ingoding gaa-izhi-gagwejimag a'aw nookomis: "Aaniin ezhiwebiziwaad wii-wiindigoowiwaad ingiw anishinaabeg, wegonen wenji-wiindigoowiwaad?
Ikidom gii-amodiwaad mewinzha."

paragraph.text_eng: This is what my grandmother said: “He who is a windigo sees the other Indians as their totems. He sees anybody who has a bear for his totem as a bear, and so he kills and eats him, and so with someone who has the deer as his totem. If anyone has a beaver as his totem, that’s how he sees him and so he kills and eats him.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod a'aw nookomis: "A'aw giiwenh waandigoowid, mii go giiwenh ezhinawaad iniw anishinaaben ezhi-wawidoodeminid.
Mii awiiya gaye makwan odoodemid, mii go makwan ezhi-izhinawaad, miinawaa mii ezhi-nisaad iniw amwaad, miinawaa iniw waawaashkeshiwan, awiiya sa go.
Amikwan awiiya go wedoodeminijin, mii i'iw ezhinawaad iniw, miish ezhi-nisaad, amwaad."

paragraph.text_eng: And she said: “When it’s beginning to be spring, perhaps in March, and it’s starting to warm up, then it melts,” she says, “the ice he must bear within himself,” she says.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash i'iw...
gii-ikido: "Ani-ziigwang, mii ganabaj a'aw onaabani-giizis, mii azhigwa ani-gagizhaateg, mii ezhi-ningizod," ikido, "maagizhaa gaye mikwamiin awiiya iidog gegishkawaagwen."

paragraph.text_eng: I asked her in vain. I don’t know about it. So he who is a windigo melts when it starts to warm up, then he recovers. He doesn’t know much of what he did previously as a windigo. That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Indaano-gii-kagwejimaa.
Gaawiin ingikendanziin.
Mii ezhi-ningizod giiwenh a'aw waandigoowid, azhigwa ani-abaatenig, mii ezhi-mikawid.
Mii gaawiin ogikendanziin iwedi minik aaniin ba-ayizhichiged wiindigoowid.
Mii sa go i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago a people way far away were called Zagwaandagaag. Those Indians are Zagwaandagaag. They’re the ones that are feared when they are hungry.

sentence.sent_text: Gichi-mewinzha giiwenh zagwaandagaag gii-inaawag iwidi akeyaa waasa.
Zagwaandagaag ingiw anishinaabeg.
Mii giiwenh ingiw gwesinjig bakadewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: A man, his wife, his three children, and his mother-in-law started off. They moved their camp far into the bush. Perhaps they killed some deer there when it was very cold. They were never seen.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go gaa-izhi-maajaad a'aw inini, wiiwan miinawaa niswi oniijaanisan miinawaa-sh iniw ozigozisan, gaa-izhi-maajaawaad.
Megwayaak iwidi waasa gii-izhi-goziwag.
Mii iwidi waawaashkeshiwan gii-nisaawaad iidog, gaa-izhi-gichi-gisinaag, iidog.
Gaawiin wiikaa gii-waabamaasiiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: Then along past the height of the winter when the snow was melting in patches, he arrived there where his fellow Indians were.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go giiwenh ingoding azhigwa go eni-giiwe-bibooninig, azhigwa go mamitanateg, gaa-izhi-dagoshing iidog imaa iniw wiiji-anishinaaben.

paragraph.text_eng: “Well, what about your wife and her children?”

sentence.sent_text: "Aaniish naa giwiiw miinawaa oniijaanisan."

paragraph.text_eng: “They all died. I'm the only one left alive,” he says. “I don’t know what was wrong with them.”

sentence.sent_text: "Mii akina gii-nibowaad.
Niineta imbimaadiz," ikido giiwenh.
"Amanj iidog gaa-inaapinewaagwen"

paragraph.text_eng: The Indians don’t leave it at that: “Well then, where did you bury them?”

sentence.sent_text: Mii gaawiin boonendanziiwag: "Aandi-sh naa gii-ningwa'wadwaa"

paragraph.text_eng: “I just put them there under the snow.”

sentence.sent_text: "Mii eta go iwidi anaamaagon gaa-izhi-asagwaa."

paragraph.text_eng: The relatives of the woman must have gone there. He led the way -- - I don’t know where they must have lived, a long way away -- and when they got to the wigwam, they (the man’s family)were lying about, scattered about in pieces. The flesh must have been chewed off their bones. There were just the bones of the dead ones there. That man must have eaten them.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ingiw wedinawemaaganijig ingiw iniw ikwewan, gaa-izhi-maajaawaad, maajaawaad.
Wiin-sh iidog igo gii-maajiizhiwe -- dibi gaa-taawaagwen, gichi-waasa -- eni-dagoshinowaad giiwenh iwidi wiigiwaaming, indigo giiwenh gaa-biiwishinowaad ingiw.
Mii eta go jiichiichiigwamaawindwaawen.
Mii eta go okanan etenigin ingiw gaa-nibojig.
Mii gii-amwaagwen a'aw inini.

paragraph.text_eng: Well, there’s nothing that could be done with him; he had turned into a windigo. It happened a while ago. Perhaps he was known to the whiteman as they were around then. It happened a while ago; not so very long ago, about a hundred years ago. Maybe he was jailed. He had turned into a windigo.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa ge-izhi'indiban; gii-wiindigoowi.
Noomaya go gii-izhiwebad i'iw.
Ganabaj ogii-kikenimigoon gichi-mookomaanan, azhigwa go eyaawaad ingiw gichi-mookomaanag.
Noomaya go gii-izhiwebad; gaawiin go aapiji noomaya, ingoji go ingodwaak gikinoonowin.
Miish ganabaj gii-kibaakwa'waa a'aw.
Gii-wiindigoowi.

chapter.eng_title: The Ones that Shot Each Other

paragraph.text_eng: More of what my grandmother told me long ago. She must have been small. She barely remembers it. All the Indians had been left behind as the men were out poling logs. They must have gotten through making syrup when the Indians who had been out poling logs came back. They brought whiskey and got drunk.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawa mewinzha gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw nookomis.
Gii-agaashiinyi ganabaj.
Agaawaa ogikendaan.
Miish giiwenh gaa-izhi-naganindwaa akina ingiw anishinaabeg, o-gaanjweba'igewaad ingiw ininiwag.
Miish giiwenh maagizhaa gaye gaa-ishkwaagamizigewaagwen, gaa-izhi-dagoshinowaad giiwenh ingiw anishinaabeg, ingiw gaa-o-gaanjweba'igejig.
Ogii-piidoonaawaa dash iidog ishkodewaaboo, gaa-izhi-giiwashkwebiiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: In the evening they heard a gun go off. There was one Indian there -- my grandmother says she barely remembers this -- that Indian, that man, running there. “They’re killing each other,” he says.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ani-onaagoshininig gaa-izhi-noondamowaad baashkizigan madwewenig.
Miish iidog maagizhaa gaye bezhig imaa anishinaabe -- agaawaa sa go ogikendaan, ikido a'aw nookomis -- bimibatoonid imaa iniw anishinaaben, ininiwan.
"Nisidiwag," ikidowan giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh, yay,” her mother says to her, “let’s go sleep someplace else,” and they must have gone and lain down in the brush as they heard the guns going off. They just listened to the frogs and went home in the morning.

sentence.sent_text: "Oo, yay," odigoon giiwenh iniw omaamaayan, "o-nibaadaa ingoji," dash iidog gaa-o-izhi-gawishimowaad megwekob mamadwewenig baashkiziganan.
Mii eta giiwenh iniw omakakiin bezindawaawaajin, azhigwa giiwenh wayaabaninig, gaa-izhi-giiwewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: They lived there in long lodges. Those Indians are laid out as if they were sleeping, maybe seven or six of them, the old lady said, as if they were sleeping.

sentence.sent_text: Gichi-ginoondawaaning gii-ayaawag, gii-taawag.
Indigo giiwenh nibaawan ezhishininid iniw anishinaaben, maagizhaa gaye niizhwaaswi, maagizhaa gaye ingodwaaswi, gii-ikido ko a'aw mindimooyen, indigo giiwenh nibaawan.

paragraph.text_eng: There was one crippled old lady there, maybe it was her mother’s mother. She was crawling around, crying. “My daughter, they shot me too,” that’s what she said. That old lady’s belt was shot right in two.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh iniw gii-mamaanjigoziwan iniw bezhig mindimooyenyan, maagizhaa gaye gaa-omaamaayigwen iniw omaamaayan.
Miish giiwenh babaamoodenid baa-mawinid.
"Indaanis ingii-paashkizogoo gaye niin," mii ko gaa-ikidod.
Mii giiwenh gaa-izhi-bakishkoodenig i'iw ogijipizon a'aw mindimooyenh.
Gaawiin idash gegoo gii-inikoozosiin, mii eta go i'iw ogijipizonigwaajigan.

paragraph.text_eng: She says that every time she hears those frogs, she thinks about when those Indians killed each other. That’s what the old lady said.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw ekidod a'aw noondawaad omakakiin noondaagozinid, ezhi-mikwendang gii-kichi-nisidiwaagobanen ingiw anishinaabeg, Mii gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: It happened because one Indian killed another man. And the brother of the one that got killed, he shot the one who had shot his brother, and so on until eight of them killed each other.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh i'iw gaa-onji-izhiwebak bezhig iidog a'aw anishinaabe ogii-nisaan ininiwan.
Miish giiwenh awedi gaye wewiijikiwenyid gaa-izhi-baashkizwaad iniw gaa-paashkizwaanijin iniw wiijikiwenyan a'aw gaa-nisind, biinish igo ishwaaswi gii-nisidiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Mii i'iw minik.

chapter.eng_title: The Ones That Shot Each Other

paragraph.text_eng: What the old lady told me long ago. She, my grandmother, was named Chi-Aakogwan.

sentence.sent_text: Gichi-mewinzha gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw mindimooyenyiban.
Gichi-aakogwan gii-izhinikaazo, mii a'aw nookomis.

paragraph.text_eng: The men used to go logging -- I don’t know where. They arrived home, so the CH goes. It is just getting dark and the women are through boiling sap; it is getting dark now and there is heard the wandering sound of drunks. My grandmother’s mother is really scared. Her great-grandmother was there too.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-kaanjweba'igewag iidog iko ingiw ininiwag -- dibi.
Miish giiwenh gaa-izhi-dagoshinowaad.
Mii azhigwa ani-dibikak, mii ishkwaa-iskigamizigewaad ingiw ikwewag; miish giiwenh azhigwa ani-dibikak, indigo giiwenh gaawanweweg gaawashkwebiijig.
Enda-zegiziwan giiwenh iniw omaamaayan a'aw nookomisiban.
Miinawaa ogichi-ookomisan iidog gii-ayaawan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh, yay,” my grandmother’s mother says. “We'd better go sleep somewhere in the brush. Let’s go sleep in the brush,” she says, she tells her. So they must have left.

sentence.sent_text: "Oonh, yay," ikido giiwenh mii iniw omaamaayan a'aw nookomis.
"Indawaaj naa ingoji o-nibaadaa megwayaak.
Daga naa ingoji o-nibaadaa megwayaak," ikido giiwenh, odigoon giiwenh.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-maajaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Then some started fighting; one of them must have shot his brother-in-law; they were arguing and one man shot his brother-in-law. They fled, my grandmother and her mother fled, they went and lay down somewhere by the meadow, they went and lay down.

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa mayaajiikodaadiwind, aya'aa-sh iidog maagizhaa gaye wiitaan, gaa-pi-baashkizwaagwen; giikaandiwaad, bezhig a'aw inini gaa-pi-izhi-baashkizwaad iniw wiitaan.
Miish gaa-izhi-ginjiba'iwewaad, mii a'aw nookomis iniw omaamaayan gaa-izhi-ginjiba'iwewaad iidog, ingoji iwidi gii-o-gawishimowaad jiigashkosiw iwidi, iwidi gii-o-gawishimowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: There were about a hundred gun shots. And a brother of the one who had been shot went there and shot another, to help his brother; and the brother of that one who had been shot went and shot another one, and so on until six (were shot), the relatives having aided each other.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoji go giiwenh ingodwaaching gii-madweweni baashkizigan.

Mii gwana go iniw wiijikiwenyini gaa-paashkizominjin, mii gaa-o-izhi-baashkizwaad, gii-o-naadamawaad iniw, mii miinawaa iniwedin bezhig a'aw wewiijikiwenyid iniw bayaashkizominjin miinawaa gaa-o-izhi-baashkizwaad, biinish igo ingodwaaswi, mii go ezhi-inawendiwaad, gaa-izhi-naadamaadiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: She must have gone to sleep listening to the frogs croaking. She must have slept, and then her mother shook her, my grandmother, awake: “Come on, let’s go home.” There is nobody to be heard fighting any more,” she tells her. They were hungry, so they went home that morning. The sap boiling lodges used to be very big. The dead ones were lying scattered around. It’s just like they’re sleeping, and the Indians are crying.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog gaa-izhi-nibaad bizindawaad iniw omakakiin noondaagozinid.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-nibaad, amajwebinigod giiwenh iniw omaamaayan a'aw nookomis: "Ambe giiwedaa.
Gaawiin geyaabi awiiya madwe-miigaadisiiwag," odigoon giiwenh.
Bakadewag igaye, gaa-izhi-giiwewaad gigizheb.
Gii-kichi-michaawan-sh ko iniw ayi'iin iskigamizige-wiigiwaaman.
Indigo giiwenh gaawanishininid iniw gaa-nisiminjin, indigo giiwenh gaawanishininid.
Indigo giiwenh nibaawan enadog, mawiwaad ingiw anishinaabeg iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: Her mother... her great-grandmother leaps up suddenly from the ground. “Waa, my daughter, look, I too have been shot at,” says that very old lady, her belt having been shot in two. She didn’t get hit. She must still be drunk. She hadn’t been hit.

sentence.sent_text: Bazigonjisewan giiwenh iniw omaamaayan...
iniw ogichi-ookomisan.
"Waa, indaanis, nashke gosha gaye niin, ingii-pwaawinaagoo," ikido giiwenh a'aw gichi-mindimooyenh, gaa-izhi-bakishkoodenig i'iw ogijipizon.
Gaawiin-sh wiin gii-miikoshkoozosiin.
Geyaabi go giiwashkwebii iidog.
Gaawiin gii-miikoshkoozosiin.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady used to say, she used to say, that every time she hears frogs, she is reminded of when that bunch of Indians killed each other.

sentence.sent_text: Miish ko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenh, miish ko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenh, endaso-noondaagoziwaad ingiw omakakiig, mii ezhi-mikwendang i'iw gichi-niibowa gii-nisidinigobanen iniw anishinaaben.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: What my grandmother used to tell me about what happened long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko a'aw nookomis gaa-izhi-waawiindamawid gaa-izhiwebak.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago there were a lot of Indians living here. There are still marks of things, whatever kind of things, where they must have lived there on the point.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha giiwenh omaa gii-taawag gichi-niibowa anishinaabeg.
Geyaabi go, mii ezhi-namesing iniw, wegodogwen iidog dinowan, dibi gaa-taawaagwen imaa neyaashiing.

paragraph.text_eng: It was her great-grandmother; she was an old lady. My grandmother’s mother must have been a little girl. She was very small. It was her great-grandmother who was paralyzed. She just sat and told stories to her.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh iniw ogichi-omaamaayibanen; ogichi-odaanikobijiganibanen; gii-mindimooyenyiwiwan.
Mii iidog igo gaa-omaamaayijin a'aw nookomis, gii-ikwezensiwiwan.
Aapiji go gii-agaashiinyiwan.
Miish giiwenh iniw ogichi-ookomisan gii-mamaanjigoziwan.
Mii eta go gii-namadabinid, ogii-inaajimotaagoon.

paragraph.text_eng: One morning as the sun is coming up, they are suddenly under attack and the Sioux are making war whoops, the Sioux are around them making war whoops. It must have been her mother’s mother or maybe her (mother’s)grandmother. This is what she says: “My daughter, go,” she tells her, “run away.” That woman must have been small. “Run, my daughter, run away.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingoding, gigizhebaawagadinig, mii azhigwa bi-mooka'aminid, baanimaa go giiwenh wenji-mawinanindwaa, bwaanan zaasaakwenid, baa-zaasaakwenid iniw bwaanan.
Miish giiwenh iidog iniw omaamaayan gaa-omaamaayinijin, maagizhaa gaye gaa-ookomisinigwen.
Miish giiwenh i'iw ekidonid: "Indaanis, maajaan," odigoon giiwenh, "maajiibatoon!"
Gii-agaashiinyiwidog a'aw ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: It must have been medicine she had in a bag, an Indian bag.

sentence.sent_text: "Maajiibatoon indaanis, maajiibatoon!"

paragraph.text_eng: “Carry this, my daughter, don’t ever throw the medicine away,” she tells her -- I don’t know what those bags must have looked like. So the girl grabbed it and started running here. This must have been my grandmother, maybe my great-grandmother, I don’t know exactly. As she runs past, she looks there where the Indians are being clubbed.

sentence.sent_text: Ayi'ii-sh iidog mashkiki, ogii-ayaan mashkimodaang, mashkimod iidog, anishinaabe-mashkimod.
"Mii o'o indaanis, bimiwidoon, gego wiikaa webinangen," odigoon giiwenh, "i'iw mashkiki" -- amanj gaa-izhinaagwadogwen iniw mashkimodan.
Miish giiwenh gaa-izhi-nawadinang a'aw ikwezens, gii-pi-maajiibatood.
Mii iidog a'aw nookomis gaye niin, maagizhaa gaye ingichi-ookomis, amanj sa iidog igo.
Miish giiwenh, azhigwa giiwenh imaa ezhi-bimibatood, akawe ko giiwenh inaabi iwidi bimi-bapakite'omind iniw anishinaaben, inaabi.

paragraph.text_eng: Suddenly somebody grabs her and hurls her around; it’s a lady. “Hurry up, come on,” she says to her. There is a meadow there. They run across it; it is spring and the buds are coming out, so they run across the meadow.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding igo giiwenh miinawaa baanimaa go giiwenh awiiya wenji-biimiskowebinigod; wegwaagi giiwenh ikwewan!
"Wewiib ambe," odigoon giiwenh.
Mashkosiw-sh imaa ayaamagad.
Mii imaa ezhi-aazhawibatoowaad; ziigwan, gii-ziigwanini, azhigwa go iidog igo zaagibagaag, gii-ziigwang, imaa mashkosiing ezhi-bimibatoowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Then they get to the other side of the meadow. “Don’t look back,” the lady says to her; she is tall. “Don’t look back,” the lady says to her. She’s tempted to. The bag hinders her. “Throw it away,” she tells her in vain. It’s the bag she carries the medicine in. When she looks back, all of the meadow, where the Indians and the children were hidden, is on fire. They could be heard crying, trapped there on the meadow by the fire.

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa giiwenh iwidi agaamashkosiw bagamiba'idiwag.
"Gego aabanaabiken," odigoon giiwenh mii iniw ikwewan; ginooziwan.
"Gego aabanaabiken," odigoon giiwenh iniw ikwewan.
Enda-zhoobizi giiwenh.
Odoondami'igon gaye i'iw mashkimod.
"Webinan," odaano-igoon giiwenh.
Mii i'iw mashkimod bemiwidood mashkiki.
Aabanaabid giiwenh imaa akina nawadidenig i'iw mashkosiw, mii imaa gii-kaazowaad ingiw anishinaabeg, ingiw abinoojiinyag gaye imaa gii-kaazowaad.
Indigo giiwenh gaa-tanweweg mewijig, mewijig, mii imaa mashkosiing gibwaakizondwaa.

paragraph.text_eng: There must be logs lying on the ground there on the hill, so she threw her behind a log lying there. She takes a look over there from under the log. “We’re being chased,” the lady tells her, lying on top of her to keep her down.

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa giiwenh imaa agidaaki, mii iidog mitigoon giiwenh imaa, bimaakoshinoon, gaa-izhi-apaginigod giiwenh imaa aagawaatig a'aw mitig imaa bimaakoshing.
Mii giiwenh iwidi wenzaabid anaamaatig.
"Gibiminizha'ogoomin," odigoon giiwenh, ezhi-minjimishkaagod, mii iniw ikwewan.

paragraph.text_eng: When she takes a look over there from under the log, sure enough a Sioux’s head is showing. The Sioux is kind of scary looking, all painted up. He looked there a little while. The sound of some guns could be heard, and some people whooping and some people crying. The Sioux looks at a long stretch of sandy beach there on the lake, but there’s nobody running away any place; they aren’t seen by the Sioux, so he turned around and ran off, running back in the direction they had come from. Soon they turn around, they turned around.

sentence.sent_text: Inaabid giiwenh iwidi anaamaatig, geget giiwenh baanimaa giiwenh wenji-zaagikweninid bwaanan.
Enda-zeginaagoziwan giiwenh, wawezhi'onid, mii iniw bwaanan.
Ajina go giiwenh imaa gii-inaabiwan.
Miish madweweg aanind baashkiziganan miinawaa zayaasaakwejig miinawaa mewijig iwidi.

Inaabid, inaabid giiwenh a'aw bwaan iwidi gichi-ginoodaawangaag imaa zaaga'iganiing, imaa weniban iwidi giiwenh ge-animiba'idiwaad ingoji; gwiinawaabamigowaad washkibagizod giiwenh a'aw bwaan gaa-izhi-maajiibatood, azhegiiwebatood akeyaa wenjibaanid.
Wayiiba go giiwenh gwekibagizowan, gaa-kwekibagizonid.

paragraph.text_eng: “Hurry up, come on,” she tells her, hurries her along holding her arm, and they ran away again. She’s so tired, that girl, she must have been small, she’s tired. “Harder,” she tells her, as they run away.

sentence.sent_text: "Wewiib, ambe," odigoon giiwenh, zaginikeba'igod, gii-maajiiba'idiwaad miinawaa.
Enda-ayekozi gaye giiwenh, mii a'aw ikwezens, gii-agaashiinyiwidog, ayekozi.
"Enigok," odigoon giiwenh, maajiiba'idiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: That must be the Mississippi over there. That lady was tall.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iwedi gichi-ziibi iidog.
Gii-kinoozi giiwenh a'aw ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: She’s looking for a place where she can cross, where they can cross the river. They had run so long it was evening; it had taken them nearly all day to run to the Mississippi. Then it’s evening, “Hurry up,” she says, and she waded across the river. She carries her on her back as she crosses the river, the Mississippi; that lady has her on her back, and again they run off.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwidi gichi-ziibi ezhi-nandawaabandaminid aandi ji-aazhoged, ji-aazhogewaad.
Mii azhigwa onaagoshininig, minik gaa-pimiba'idiwaad; gegaa gabe-giizhik gii-pimiba'idiwag gichi-ziibiing.
Miish azhigwa onaagoshininig, "Wewiib," ikidowan giiwenh gaa-izhi-aazhawagaaziinid, mii i'iw ziibi.
Miish giiwenh ezhi-bimoomigod aazhawagaanid, mii i'iw ziibi, gichi-ziibi, ezhi-bimoomigod iniw ikwewan, miinawaa gii-maajiiba'idiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: They didn’t sleep at all. They went there to Leech Lake. There were some Indians there. That’s where they went, where they’re going. They ran for two days.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin booch gii-nibaasiiwag.
Miish iwidi gaa-izhaawaad iidog ayi'ing gaa-zagaskwaajimekaag.
Aanind anishinaabeg gii-ayaawag.
Miish iwidi gaa-izhaawaad, ezhaawaad.
Niizhogon giiwenh gii-pimiba'idiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: The lady doesn’t sleep; when she (the girl)tries to sleep, she wakes her up, “Hurry let’s go tell.” She knows they ran for two days.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go gaawiin nibaasiin a'aw ikwe; aano-nibaad giiwenh ezhi-amajwebinigod; "Wewiib, o-dibaajimodaa."
Niizhogon sa go ogikendaan, gii-pimiba'idiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: After arriving where the Indians were, they tell them. Only those two were left alive of the Indians dwelling at Mille Lacs. Some of those Indians there at Leech Lake started off for here. Those Indians came here. Many of their relatives there had been killed. The girl cries constantly, she constantly cries as they walk.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iwidi gaa-izhi-dagoshinowaad iniw anishinaaben gii-ayaanid, dibaajimowaad giiwenh.
Mii eta niizh bimaadiziwaad minik imaa misi-zaaga'iganiing gaa-taawaad ingiw anishinaabeg.
Miish giiwenh miinawaa gii-pi-maajaawaad ingiwedig aanind anishinaabeg gaa-zagaskwaajimekaag.
Miish giiwenh gaa-pi-izhi-maajaawaad iwidi ingiw anishinaabeg.
Odinawemaaganiwaan imaa gii-paatayiinowan imaa iniw gaa-nisiminjin.
Mii go apane ezhi-mawid, mii a'aw ikwezens, apane ezhi-bimademod bimosewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: It took them two days to walk back here to where the Indians had lived. There were only maggots, lying an inch thick. The maggots lay an inch thick, she used to tell. The woman’s grandmother, my grandmother’s great-grandmother, the crippled one, that old lady was just cut to pieces. “I wondered why,” she used to say, “she had been cut to pieces. Perhaps she stabbed a Sioux, it was said. That’s why they cut the old lady like that.”

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa giiwenh gii-niizhogon giiwenh imaa gii-tazhitaawag wii-pi-azhegiiwewaad, gii-bimosewaad imaa, gii-izhaawaad, azhigwa giiwenh degoshinowaad imaa anishinaaben gaa-taanid.
Mii go giiwenh, mii eta go giiwenh aya'aag ookweg ingodoninj gii-apiichishinoog.
Miish ingiw ookweg ingodoninj gii-apiichishinoog, gii-inaajimo ko.
Miish giiwenh iniw ookomisan a'aw ikwe, a'aw nookomis iniw ogichi-ookomisan memaanjigozinijin, mii go giiwenh gaa-izhi-wenda-bigishkizhond a'aw mindimooyenh.
"Amanj i'iw," gii-ikido ko, "gii-pigishkizhond Ganabaj ogii-pazhiba'waan bwaanan, gii-ikidom iko.
Mii a'aw mindimooyenh, miish gaa-onji-inizhond."

paragraph.text_eng: That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: What my grandmother used to tell me about her older brother long ago. I barely remember him. He was an old man.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko a'aw nookomis gaa-inaajimotawid osayenyan.
Agaawaa ingezikwenimaa a'aw akiwenzii.
Gii-kichi-akiwenziiyiwi.

paragraph.text_eng: And this is what she told me. That old man was bald. He must have been sick. He whispered. He could hardly be heard when he talked.

sentence.sent_text: Miish miinawaa gaa-inaajimotawid Gii-waabizhagindibe a'aw akiwenzii.
Gii-aakozi iidog.
Gii-kaaskanazo gaye.
Agaawaa go gii-noondawaa gaagiigidod.

paragraph.text_eng: She told about long ago when he was a young man. My grandmother must have been a little girl then. But her older brother was a young man then.

sentence.sent_text: Miish gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenh mewinzha giiwenh gii-oshki-ininiiwid.
Gii-ikwezensiwi-sh iidog a'aw nookomis.
Gii-oshki-ininiiwiwan-sh wiin iniw osayenyan.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago the Sioux used to gamble with them, before they fought each other. It was there over by what is called Gaa-zhaagawashkodeyaag (Long Prairie), over that way, way off. Not so very far away.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko giiwenh ingiw bwaanag mewinzha, gaa-izhi-ataadiwaad jibwaa-miigaadiwaad igo.
Miish iwidi gaa-zhaagawashkodeyaag izhi-wiinde, iwidi akeyaa, waasa.
Gaawiin go aapiji waasawasinoon.

paragraph.text_eng: Those Sioux gambled all their belongings. They gambled their wives and also their children. That old man, he didn’t have many children, maybe he just had two of them. Maybe he had two horses, maybe he had three of them. You see, long ago they travelled along only on horseback, they always just travelled along on horseback.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingiw bwaanag gii-ataadiwaad akina go gegoo odaniwiniwaan.
Mii ezhi-ataadiwaad wiiwiwaan igo gaye miinawaa go iniw oniijaanisiwaan.

Miish gaye wiin iidog a'aw akiwenzii, gaawiin igo gii-paatayiinisiiwan, maagizhaa gaye gaa-niizhinigwen iniw oniijaanisan, mii a'aw akiwenzii, Odayan, maagizhaa gaye gaa-niizhinigwen, maagizhaa gaye gaa-nisinigwen.
Aaniish naa gii-pimoomigowag eta mewinzha, apane gii-pimoomigowaad eta go.

paragraph.text_eng: They went over there to Long Prairie to live, and the Sioux and the Chippewa had races with each other; the Chippewa go there to gamble, to bet with the Sioux.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh iwidi we'o-daawaad gaa-zhaagawashkodeyaag, gagwejikanidiwaad ingiw bwaanag miinawaa ingiw anishinaabeg; o-ataagewaad ingiw ojibwewanishinaabeg, o-atawaawaad iniw bwaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: There’s this one Sioux; he’s really big. He and the old man bet with each other, says the old lady. So they took off running a long way across the clearing. It must be a distance of two miles that they had to run. It is said, by those who were watching, that the Sioux nearly caught up to the old man when he was halfway. Those who watched said that there was a leaf tumbling along. That’s all they saw, a leaf tumbling along. When they arrived there, when they ran up there, the old man was standing there giving a big war whoop.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh azhigwa bezhig iniw bwaanan; enda-mindidowan giiwenh.
Miish igo gaa-izhi-ataadiwaad, mii a'aw akiwenaii, ikido a'aw mindimooyenh.
Miish giiwenh azhigwa gaa-izhi-maajiiba'idiwaad, waasa-sh giiwenh, waasa izhi-mizhishawaamagad.
Maagizhaa gaye niizho-diba'igan waasa sa iidog da-apa'idiwag.
Miish giiwenh i'iw ekidong a'aw akiwenzii, ingiw gaa-kanawaabamaajig, aayaabita giiwenh eni-ayaad, gegaa ogii-adimigoon iniw bwaanan.
Miish ingiw gaa-kanawaabamaajig ayi'ii giiwenh i'iw aniibiishibag i'iw gaa-ani-ditibibideg, gii-ikidowag, Azhigwa, mii eta go gii-waabandamowaad aniibiishibag bimi-ditibibidenig iidog.
Azhigwa iwidi begamiba'idiwaad akeyaa ge-apa'idiwaad iidog, begamibatoowaad, gii-niibawi giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii gichi-zaasaakwed.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady used to tell about, how he beat that Sioux.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenh, gaa-izhi-bakinawaad iniw bwaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago my grandmother used to tell me about there where the lakes almost touch; that lake is called Zezabegamag (Bay Lake). There were about a hundred wigwams of Indians there, Chippewas.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko a'aw mindimooyenh gaa-inaajimotawid iwidi iidog wabigamaag; zezabegamaag izhinikaade zaaga'igan.
Mii iidog iwidi ingodwaak gii-tasogamiziwag ingiw anishinaabeg, ojibwewanishinaabeg.

paragraph.text_eng: There was one lady; she was a widow. A long time ago this is what they did when somebody’s husband died. The widow, the lady, keeps her husband’s belongings.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog bezhig a'aw ikwe, gii-shiigaawi.
Mewinzha-sh iidog, mii i'iw akeyaa gaa-izhichiged awiiya nibonid onaabeman.
Mii gegoo odayi'iimini ezhi-ganawendang a'aw zhiigaa, a'aw ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what they believe. Her husband is still there, staying with her. After a year she collects together all sorts of things, blankets, maybe beadwork. When she gets through, she summons her husband’s associates -- - his relatives, for example, his brothers, his younger brothers and sisters, his older sisters, those closely related to him -- - and has a give-away. She is looked after, clothed properly, made up, and her hair is dressed.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw enendamowaad.
Mii go geyaabi ezhi-ayaanid imaa iniw onaabeman, wiiji-ayaawigod.
Baanimaa dash igo ingo-gikinoonowin, mii i'iw asiginang sa go akina gegoo, waabooyaanan, maagizhaa gaye manidoominensikaanan.
Miish giizhiitaad, mii ezhi-nandomaad iniw onaabemibanen wiiji-aya'aani -- odinawemaaganini, dibishkoo go wiijikiwenyini, oshiimeyini, omisenyini, besho sa go enawemaanijin -- giiweniged.
Miish ezhi-nanaa'inind, biizikonaye'ind weweni, wawezhi'ind, miinawaa nazikwe'ond.

paragraph.text_eng: Then she is through taking care of her husband and she can do what she wants. The lady is through being taken care of. She has given presents to everyone for him, as if she is paying his relatives for him.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw bijiinag ezhi-ishkwaa-ganawenimaad iniw onaabeman ge-wii-izhichiged igo.
Mii i'iw gii-ishkwaa-ganawendaagozid a'aw ikwe.
Mii i'iw akina gii-kiiwenamawaad, dibishkoo go odiba'amawaan iniw gaa-inawemaanijin,

paragraph.text_eng: One morning this lady went after water and saw a wolf running across the channel. Then another one runs across. So she went inland; they were staying there with an old man.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash giiwenh ingoding gigizheb nibinaadid a'aw ikwe gaa-izhi-waabamaad ma'iinganan aazhoobatoonid iwidi wabi-ayaanig.
Miinawaa go giiwenh bezhig aazhoobatoowan.
Mii giiwenh gaa-izhi-gopiid; akiwenziinyan dash imaa ogii-wiiji-ayaawaawaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what she says: “Grandfather, I see some wolves. There are lots of them running across the channel.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw ekidod, "Ma'iinganag niwaabamaag, nimishoo.
Enda-niibowa aazhooba'idiwag iwidi wabi-ayaag."

paragraph.text_eng: “My granddaughter,” the old man says, “they are the Sioux.”

sentence.sent_text: "Noozis," ikido giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii, "Bwaanag ingiw."

paragraph.text_eng: The old man called out to the Indians: “There is danger; the Sioux are attacking us.” As he’s saying that, the Sioux give war whoops and attack them.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh gaa-izhi-biibaagimaad iniw anishinaaben a'aw akiwenzii: "Baapiniziwaagan, bwaanag gidoodisigonaanig."
Mii go giiwenh ezhi-ikidod zaasaakwenid bwaanan, mawinanigowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: There was a pine tree there, so the widow went up to it and threw that thing she kept up against it. “Take care of me,” she says to it, and she climbed up that pine. From there she looked down at the Indians being killed. The Indians (Chippewas)were all wiped out. They killed some of the Sioux. She stays up there in the tree watching the Sioux.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh a'aw zhiigaa, zhingwaak giiwenh imaa badakizo gaa-izhi-aatwaakowebinang i'iw genawendang, "Ganawenimishin," odidaan giiwenh, gaa-izhi-akwaandawed imaa zhingwaakong.
Miish imaa gaa-onzaabid niiwana'omind iniw anishinaaben.
Mii go akina gaa-izhi-jaaginanindwaa ingiw anishinaabeg.
Aanind ogii-nisaawaan iniw bwaanan.
Miish giiwenh imaa ayagoozid imaa zhingwaakong ganawaabamaad iniw bwaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: It must have been spring as it was open along the shore. The Sioux cut a hole in the ice there on the lake. It is there that they had a mass burial, there in the hole.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-siigwan iidog, jiigewezhaagigamiiwan.
Miish giiwenh iniw bwaanan gaa-izhi-dwaa'igenid imaa zaaga'iganiing.
Miish imaa gii-piinjwebinidinid imaa dwaa'ibaaning.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady, my grandmother, said: “The trees still have the scars on them,” she said. It didn’t happen so very long ago. This is what she told. That lady wasn’t seen by the Sioux. She was the only one left alive. That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenh, nookomis, "Mii go geyaabi ezhi-wawijiishigiwaad ingiw mitigoog," gii-ikido.
Gaawiin mewinzha aapiji gii-izhiwebasinoon.
Mii go gaa-inaajimod.
Miish giiwenh a'aw ikwe, mii go gaawiin ogii-waabamigosiin iniw bwaanan.
Mii eta a'aw gaa-pimaadizid.
Mii i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Once my grandmother and I were driving by Bay Lake and she pointed out to me the big point there at the channel. “Over there,” she says, “there were a lot of Indians living there on the other side of the lake,” she says. “There was one lady carrying the bundle,” she said, “a widow. She had lost her husband; they keep something, maybe his shirt, or maybe a suit of clothes tied together. The woman takes care of it, and also feeds it, taking it along wherever she goes. The Indians long ago said that she thinks that’s where she keeps her husband, that’s what they said long ago.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwidi ani-bimidaabii'iweyaang a'aw nookomis zezabegamaag gaa-izhi-izhinoo'amawid iwidi gichi-neyaashiiwan iwidi wabi-ayaamagad.
"Mii iwidi," ikido, "niibowa imaa anishinaabeg gii-taawag imaa awasayi'ii awasagaam," ikido.
"Miish giiwenh a'aw ikwe bezhig ganawendaaso," gii-ikido, "zhiigaa.
Ogii-wani'aan onaabeman; ganawendamowaad gegoo maagizhaa gaye obagiwayaanini, maagizhaa gaye ingodwewaan biizikiiganan ezhi-dakobidoowaad.
Miish ezhi-ganawendang a'aw ikwe ezhi-ganawendang, odashandaan igaye miinawaa, mii go ezhaad ezhiwidood.
Mii i'iw enendang gaa-ikidowaad mewinzha anishinaabeg, mii imaa ishkonaad iniw onaabeman gii-ikidowag mewinzha."

paragraph.text_eng: In the morning once a young woman going after water saw wolves there at the channel. She watches the wolves attempt to run across the channel, and then she went a ways inland. There was an old man sitting nearby. You see, they are having breakfast as it is just beginning to be morning. “I wonder why I am seeing a lot of wolves running across over there,” she says.

sentence.sent_text: Mii giiwenh gigizheb ingoding nibinaadid bezhig oshkiniigikwe, gaa-izhi-waabamaad ma'iinganan, mii imaa wabi-ayaanig.
Aano-aazhooba'idiwan giiwenh ma'iinganan, aano-aazhooba'idiwan giiwenh ma'iinganan imaa, gaganawaabamaad ingoding giiwenh azhigwa gomaa go minik gaa-izhi-gopiid.
Besho go imaa akiwenzii namadabi imaa.
Aaniish naa gigizhebaa-wiisiniwag, mii bijiinag gigizhebaawagadinig.
"Amanaa gaye enda-niibowa niwaabamaag ma'iinganag iwidi aazhogeba'idiwaad," ikido giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: “Hey, there is cause for alarm,” the old man says, shouting. “The Sioux are attacking us.” He no more than says that and the Sioux are upon them.

sentence.sent_text: "He, baapiniziwaagan, baapiniziwaagan," ikido giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii, baabiibaagid.
"Bwaanag gimawinanigonaanig."
Mii go ezhi-ikidod, mii azhigwa imaa ingiw bwaanag bagamiba'idiwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: That lady who is taking care of her husband throws it (the bundle)up on a pine tree. “Take care of me if you are really there,” she says and she climbed up the pine. That’s where she perched as she watched her relatives get killed. Nothing whatever happened to her.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh a'aw ikwe genawenimaad iniw onaabeman ani-izhi-apagidang imaa zhingwaakong.
"Ganawenimishin, ganawenimishin geget imaa eyaawanen," ikido giiwenh gaa-izhi-akwaandawebatood imaa zhingwaakong.
Miish iwidi gii-ayagoozid, ganawaabamaad imaa niiwana'omind iniw odinawemaaganan.
Gaawiin giiwenh gegoo gii-izhiwebizisiin giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: All of the Indians who lived there were killed. It is said that the Sioux chopped holes in the ice. That’s where they threw them (the bodies). A lot of them were killed. A lot of Sioux were killed there too.

sentence.sent_text: Akina gaa-izhi-niiwana'omind imaa iniw imaa gaa-taajig anishinaabeg.
Miish giiwenh gaa-ikidong, mii i'iw giiwenh gaa-izhi-dwaa'igewaad ingiw imaa ingiw bwaanag.
Miish imaa gii-piinjwebinidiwaad.
Niibowa gaye wiinawaa gii-nisaawag.
Niibowa gaye imaa gii-nisaawag ingiw bwaanag.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what my late grandmother said. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii gaa-ikidod a'aw nookomisiban.
Mii sa go i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what the old lady said: “Even recently,” she says, “there were signs of the hatchets used to try to pin people up against the trees, maybe some of the Indians there. The trees there have grown up scarred,” the old lady said.

sentence.sent_text: Mii i'iw ekidod a'aw mindimooyenh: "Noomaya go geyaabi," ikido, "mii go eyezhishing iniw waagaakwadoonsan, aano-gii-ayaagwaakoba'iwewaad ganabaj ingiw imaa, ingiw anishinaabeg aanind.
Miish giiwenh ingiw mitigoog imaa izhi-maamaakigiwaad," gii-ikido a'aw mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago my grandmother told me about, maybe it’s her mother’s mother, and how all the women were left alone to boil sap there at the sap boiling place as it is called, while the men went logging. Across the lake was the old lady’s mother, at what is called Gichi-neyaashiing ‘The Big Point’.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw nookomis iniw iidog omaamaayibanen omaamaayini, gaa-izhi-naganindwaa giiwenh akina ikwewag iskigamizigewaad -- iskigamiziganing izhi-wiinde -- o-gaanjweba'igewaad ingiw ininiwag.
Agaaming iidog iwidi gii-ayaawan iniw omaamaayan a'aw mindimooyenh, gichi-neyaashiing izhi-wiindenig.

paragraph.text_eng: One evening she is carrying sap. I don’t know where they got those barrels -- - they called them atoobaanan. While she was pouring and straining sap, she saw the reflection of a Sioux in the sap. She wasn’t afraid, so she turned around, and went inside. When they go to sleep, the sound of someone walking around outside is heard; someone is rustling and parting the cattail mat trying to peek at them. She wasn’t scared.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ingoding iniw onaagoshininig naadoobiid.
Dibi dash gaa-ondinamowaagwen iniw makakosagoon -- atoobaanan ogii-izhi-wiindaanaawaan.
Miish giiwenh imaa ziiginang ziikoobiiginang i'iw wiishkobaaboo, gaa-izhi-waabamaad bwaanan ojichaagobiishininid.
Gaawiin-sh giiwenh gii-segizisiin, gaa-izhi-washkigaabawid gaa-izhi-biindiged.
Mii giiwenh azhigwa nibaawaad, noondawaawaad iniw bebaamweweshininijin imaa agwajiing miinawaa apakweshkwayan gaaskibinaanid, dawibinaanid, gagwe-giimaabamigowaad awiiya.
Miish iidog gaawiin gii-segizisiin.

paragraph.text_eng: When daylight came, they started to work. Then again it is night; she woke up once in the night and saw someone seated there, someone giggling, whispering, playing with the fire. She is disturbed and scared; as she turned over they ran out. She saw two run out giggling, then she got up intending to put on her leggings, but they must have been placed on the fire as they were burnt in half. She wasn’t scared.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go miinawaa wayaabaninig gaa-izhi-maajitaawaad anokiiwaad.
Azhigwa miinawaa debikadinig, ingoding igo giiwenh goshkozid niibaadibik, gaa-izhi-waabamaad nemadabinijin, genagaapinijin sa go, gaaskanazonid, dazhiikaminid i'iw ishkode.
Enda-ishkendam giiwenh, zegizi; gaa-izhi-gwekishing, gaa-izhi-zaagiziba'idinid.
Niizh ogii-waabamaan ani-ginagaapinid gaa-izhi-onishkaad, wii-piizikang iniw odaasan, gaa-achigaadenigwen giiwenh imaa ishkodeng gaagiishkaakidenig iniw odaasan.
Miish giiwenh gaawiin gii-segizisiin.

paragraph.text_eng: There must have been Indians there, perhaps three lodges of them, I don’t know exactly. There was one short lady. They thought of her as having spiritual power, and she told her: “Perhaps there are Sioux there,” she said to her, she told that woman.

sentence.sent_text: Anishinaabeg-sh iidog imaa gii-ayaawag, maagizhaa gaye gaa-nisogamiziwaagwen, amanj idash iidog igo.
Bezhig giiwenh ikwe enda-dakoozi.
Ogii-manidookenaawaan gaa-izhi-wiindamawaad: "Ganabaj bwaanag imaa ayaawag," ogii-inaan, ogii-wiindamawaan iniw ikwewan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Don’t be afraid,” she said back to her. “Nothing will happen to us.” Then she had no further thought of being scared.

sentence.sent_text: "Gego zegiziken," odigoon giiwenh.
"Gaawiin gegoo gidaa-izhiwebizisiimin."
Miish giiwenh gaawiin ogii-pabaamendanziin ji-zegizid.

paragraph.text_eng: Then it was morning again and it must have been snowing.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh miinawaa wayaabaninig, gaa-izhi-zoogiponinigwen

paragraph.text_eng: There were tracks of a man outside, but only of one. She said that there must have been three of those Sioux stepping in the same tracks. They had gone away so perhaps they had taken pity on them as they might have killed them.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-bimikawewan imaa agwajiing ininiwan, mii eta go bezhig.
Miish iko gaa-ikidod maagizhaa gaye gaa-nisinigwen gii-naaba'anidizowan iniw bwaanan.
Mii sa apane gii-maajaanid, maagizhaa gaye gaa-shawenimigowaagwen, ji-gii-naaniiwana'ogowaapan.

paragraph.text_eng: That is what my grandmother told.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa i'iw gaa-inaajimod a'aw nookomis.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago the old lady used to tell me all kinds of stories; when I sleep with her she tells things, she tells me about things. “It was a long time ago,” she says, “there at what they call Giigoonh-zhagomod (Stillwater, Minnesota),” she says.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko a'aw mindimooyenh anooj ingii-inaajimotaag; wiipemag iko, dadibaajimod, dibaajimotawid.
"Miish giiwenh mewinzha" ikido "iwidi giigoonh-zhagomod izhi-wiindemagak, giigoonh agomod," ikido.

paragraph.text_eng: Once long ago there were two men sleeping, one being the other’s brother-in-law, perhaps they were setting traps around there. Long ago they used to sell furs.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh mewinzha niizh ininiwag, bezhig giiwenh wiitaan iidog, nibaawaad, maagizhaa gaye baa-wanii'igewaad.
Mewinzha ko gii-adaawaagewaad iidog adaawaaganan.

paragraph.text_eng: That man killed a fish; one of the men killed and cooked a fish. Well, he’s hungry. His brother-in-law was also hungry.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh giigoonyan gaa-izhi-nisaad, mii a'aw inini; a'aw bezhig giigoonyan gaa-izhi-nisaad, gabaashimaad.
Aaniish naa bakade giiwenh.
Gaye wiin a'aw bakadewan iniw wiitaan.

paragraph.text_eng: “There’s no way I can eat that fish, that pike,” the other one told him. “I can’t eat it,” his brother-in-law says to him.

sentence.sent_text: "Gaawiin ganage indaa-amwaasiin a'aw giigoonh," odigoon giiwenh, "ginoozhe.
Gaawiin indaa-amwaasiin a'aw," odinaan giiwenh iniw wiitaan.

paragraph.text_eng: “Well, you’re just going to have to eat it anyway.”

sentence.sent_text: "Haw, booch sa go ji-amwad."

paragraph.text_eng: “Don’t! I don’t want to eat it.”

sentence.sent_text: "Gego, gaawiin niwii-amwaasiin."

paragraph.text_eng: He coaxed his brother-in-law to eat it. Then that man said: “Don’t you dare go to sleep, don’t go to sleep. Just go and keep on dipping up water so I can eat the fish,” he says to him.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa giiwenh gaa-izhi-gagaandinoonaad iniw wiitaan ji-amwaanid.
Miish giiwenh ekidod a'aw inini bezhig: "Gego sa naa nibaaken, gego sa naa nibaaken.
Mii eta go apane o-gwaaba'an i'iw nibi ji-amwag a'aw giigoonh," odinaan giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: Then, sure enough, when it got dark, he ate the fish. “Heh, my brother-in-law, I’m thirsty,” he says to him. All that man does then is keep dipping up water in the pail. All the other man, his brother-in-law, does is drink up the pail.

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa giiwenh geget, azhigwa, dibikadinig, mii gii-amwaad iniw giigoonyan.
"He niit, ingiishkaabaagwe," odinaan giiwenh.
Mii sa giiwenh apane azhigwa, mii eta go gwaaba'ang i'iw nibi a'aw inini akikong.
Mii go wewiib ezhi-ziikaapidang a'aw inini, iniw wiitaan, iniw akikong, mii eta go epiichitaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Then it was dawn and the one bringing the water fell asleep. He woke up with a start and his brother-in-law was gone.

sentence.sent_text: Mii giiwenh azhigwa biidaabaninig, gaa-izhi-gawingwashid, mii a'aw, mii a'aw nebinaadid, gaa-izhi-gawingwashid.
Mii giiwenh gaa-izhi-amajised giiwenh, weniban giiwenh iniw wiitaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Then there was his brother-in-law, floating across the lake. The big fish floating there told him this. This is what it told him: “You will know that I will be there from henceforth. There at what will be called Giigoonh-agomod ‘Where the Fish Floats’, he told him.

sentence.sent_text: Mii giiwenh azhigwa, mii giiwenh azhigwa gii-kiizhagomonid ezhi-aazhawaakwagomonid imaa zaaga'iganiing, mii iniw wiitaan.
Miish giiwenh i'iw egod gichi-giigoonh imaa gii-agomo.
Miish giiwenh i'iw egod: "Mii imaa ge-ani-danenimiyan.
Mii imaa giigoonh-agomod ge-izhi-wiindeg," odigoon giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: The lake must still look that way today. There must be a piece of land crossing the lake there.

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo noongom ezhi-naagwadogwen i'iw zaaga'igan.
Gichi-aazhawakamigaadog imaa zaaga'igan.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go i'iw minik.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady used to tell me about all sorts of things. It’s like this: they were sleeping at Garrison once. The Indians used to sleep all over on their way around picking berries or out fishing, living here and there. They never stayed in one place. They just moved along, camping all sorts of places.

sentence.sent_text: Anooj iko ingii-inaajimotaag a'aw mindimooyenh.
Nashke gaye imaa mazhii'iganing nibaawaad iidog aabiding.
Miziwe ko gii-pimi-nibaawag anishinaabeg, baa-mawinzowaad, maagizhaa gaye baa-wewebanaabiiwaad, baa-daawaad sa go gaye.
Gaawiin wiikaa bezhigwanong gii-ayaasiiwag.
Mii eta go gii-pimi-goziwaad, anooj igo izhi-goziwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: When they were sleeping there at the place called Garrison, a heavy thunderstorm came up, a great storm. There was continuous lightning. It was like daylight. When they took a look, something was there, something visible and moving away in the lightning. It was very big and very long, and they were scared when they beheld what was happening, a piece of land was making a wake, a piece of land was moving off. They wondered what was going on, as the lightning continued moving off in the direction of Minisaabikong ‘Rock Island’ (Spirit Island), as it moved off with lightning bolts strung across the sky. She said she didn’t know who it was (that caused that).

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog imaa nibaawaad imaa, mii imaa mazhii'iganing ezhi-wiindeg, gaa-izhi-gichi-animikiikaanig giiwenh, gichi-nichiiwadinig giiwenh.
Mii sa giiwenh ezhi-wenda-go-aabiji-waasesenig.
Mii go ezhi-giizhigadinig.
Mii naa iwidi enaabiwaad iidog giiwenh gegoo gaa-ani-ayaanig gaa-ani-naagwadinig, ezhi-waasesenig.
Enda-michaani giiwenh, enda-ginwaani, zegiziwaad giiwenh enaabiwaad aaniin ezhiwebak ani-daadobiinig, akiish i'iw, aki iidog i'iw, animi-ayaanig.
Miish giiwenh wegodogwen apane giiwenh iwidi ani-wawaasesenig apane giiwenh iwidi akeyaa minisaabikong, apane giiwenh inaabiwin eni-inaabiigagoodenig imaa.
Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod awegwen a'aw.

paragraph.text_eng: When they woke up there was a creek there where they would have to drive. It’s very deep. That’s where they drive across. It’s very deep there.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh gweshkoziwaad goda, gii-ayaani giiwenh imaa ziibiins imaa ayaanig, imaa ge-ani-izhidaabii'iwewaad.
Enda-dimiini.
Mii ko imaa bimi-aazhogedaabii'iwewaad i'iw.
Enda-dimiini imaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Gone, gone was the land there; a piece of land must have split off there and the Indians were surprised. Where had it gone? I wonder what sort of manitou had taken off from there, she used to say.

sentence.sent_text: Weniban giiwenh, weniban giiwenh imaa i'iw aki, gomaa go minik gaa-izhi-bakweshkaanigwen imaa, biinge'endamowaad ingiw anishinaabeg.
Aandi gaa-inikaag i'iw ayi'ii?
Awegwen dinowa manidoo imaa gaa-maajaagwen gii-ikido ko.

paragraph.text_eng: It went over there to Minisaabikong. It is still there. It is never dry there where the land split off.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iwidi minisaabikong gaa-izhaad.
Ayaamagad-sh igo geyaabi i'iw.
Mii imaa gaawiin wiikaa iskaabiisinoon imaa gii-pakweshkaag i'iw aki.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady used to tell. That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Mii i'iw gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.
Mii i'iw minik.

paragraph.text_eng: Again long ago, it must be when my grandmother was a young lady, maybe she was married, I don’t really know. Right there at what’s called Garrison, that’s where they slept. They slept at Mille Lacs Lake in the summer, on their way looking for groundhogs. They used to eat them. It must have been there that they went to sleep towards evening.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa-sh gichi-mewinzha, nookomis iidog gii-oshkiniigikwewid igo, maagizhaa gaye gaa-wiidigegwen, amanj iidog igo.
Miish iidog imaa ayi'ing mazhii'iganing izhi-wiindeg, mii iidog imaa gaa-izhi-nibaawaad.
Anooj igo gii-pimi-nibaawag niibininig, imaa misi-zaaga'iganiing, nandawaabamaawaad gaye akakojiishensan.
Ogii-amwaawaan iko.
Mii iidog imaa gaa-izhi-nibaawaad ini-onaagoshininig.

paragraph.text_eng: Well, they’re on foot, carrying packs, or maybe they’re paddling. It must have been late in the evening when they went to sleep there, having set up something -- - I don’t know what, maybe their mosquito bars or maybe little tents. Then late at night, lightning comes. They must have gone to sleep and woken up in a great storm with the manitous flashing lightning.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa mitosewag, bimiwanewag, maagizhaa gaye bimishkaawag.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-onaagoshininig imaa gaa-izhi-nibaawaad, gaa-izhi-onakidoowaad iniw -- wegodogwen iidog dinowan, maagizhaa gaye ozagimewayaaniwaan, maagizhaa gaye bagiwayaanegamigoonsan.
Mii iidog azhigwa ishpi-dibikadinig bi-wawaasesenig.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-nibaawaad gaa-izhi-goshkoziwaad gichi-nichiiwadinig, gichi-wawaasaminid iniw manidoon.

paragraph.text_eng: They must have gone out to see what was going to happen. They must have seen a piece of land split off, a lot of it. It starts moving off. The lightning keeps striking it. That lightning goes out along toward the lake, always going straight to Minisaabikong ‘Rock Island’ (Spirit Island).

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog gaa-izhi-zaaga'amowaad iko waabandamowaad aaniin ge-izhiwebadinig.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-waabandamowaad imaa aki bakweshkaanig, niibowa go.
Miish gaa-izhi-maajiishkaamagadinig.
Miish iidog i'iw waasamowin, mii apane imaa enaabiigisenig.
Mii i'iw waasamowin bimi-ayaamagadinig imaa zaaga'iganiing apane giiwenh gwayak iwidi minisaabikong.

paragraph.text_eng: When the storm was over, they slept. In the morning when they woke up: “Take a look here at what it looks like,” they say. Now there is a stream there. It’s never dry there. A great hunk of land must have broken off there.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog eshkwaa-nichiiwadinig, gaa-izhi-nibaawaad.
Gigizheb giiwenh gweshkoziwaad: "Nashke gosha naa omaa izhinaagwak," ikidowag giiwenh.
Ziibiins imaa noongom dagon.
Gaawiin wiikaa ayaasinoon iskaabiisinoon imaa.
Enda-gichi-niibowa imaa gii-pakweshkaadog i'iw aki.

paragraph.text_eng: It is still there where that land came off. “Wonder who it was that ran away,” they used to say long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo geyaabi imaa ezhi-ayaamagak i'iw aki gaa-onji-maajiishkaamagak.
"Awegwen imaa gaa-kinjiba'iwegwen," gii-ikidowag iko mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa go i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: There was said to have been an old woman, a witch. She wore metal shoes.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig giiwenh a'aw mindimooyenyish gii-ayaagoban, maji-mindimooyenyish.
Biiwaabikwakizinensan giiwenh ogii-piizikaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: Once the old woman says: “It is called ‘Onamia’ -- Naaniimi’aa -- because I danced around there [ningii-tazhi-naaniim].” She was a very evil witch. If she is seen about somewhere, no one would laugh and no one would speak. No one would smile at her or do anything at all.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingoding, "Mii i'iw wenji-izhinikaadeg niin i'iw Onamia -- naaniimi'aa -- ingii-naaniim imaa, ingii-tazhi-naaniim," ikido giiwenh a'aw mindimooyenyish.
Gii-wenda-gichi-maji-aya'aawishiwi.
Gaawiin awiiya daa-gii-paapisiin, miinawaa ingoji waabamind, gaawiin awiiya daa-gaagiigidosiin.
Gaawiin gaye awiiya odaa-zhoomiingwetawaasiin, gaawiin sa go gegoo.

paragraph.text_eng: Once there were two young people, newly married, who had a little baby. I don’t know what the woman must have done, but she laughed at her husband as they were sitting down; that woman burst into laughter. I don’t know what her husband must have done, but she laughed at him.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingoding, niizh gii-oshki-wiidigendiwag iidog, mii oshki-aya'aag, gaa-izhi-oniijaanisensiwaad.
Amanj iidog gaa-izhichigegwen a'aw ikwe, iniw onaabeman ogii-paapi'aan namadabiwaad, gaa-izhi-baashkaapid giiwenh a'aw ikwe.
Amanj gaa-izhichigenigwen iniw onaabeman, ogii-paapi'aan.

paragraph.text_eng: The evil old woman is sitting there looking hard at the laughers.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh imaa a'aw mindimooyenyish namadabid, gichi-ganawaabamaad giiwenh, gichi-ganawaabamaad, mii iniw bayaapinijin.

paragraph.text_eng: “I’m being laughed at.” she’s thinking.

sentence.sent_text: "Imbaapi'igoo," inendam.

paragraph.text_eng: Then, once, I don’t know how many days later, she was there where they were having a dance, maybe it was the Midewiwin, I don’t know. There was some event. They are sitting in front feeling bad about having lost their little child. She’s dancing there with that child stuffed and used as her medicine pouch, shaking as if it were fringed.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ingoding gaa-izhi-ayaad, amanj igo endasogonagak, gaa-izhi-niimi'iding, maagizhaa gaye gaa-midewiwiingen, amanj iidog.
Gegoo sa wiin igo gii-inakamigad.
Mii giiwenh imaa enaasamabinid iniw, maanendaminid iniw gaa-wani'aanijin iniw oniijaanisensini.
Mii giiwenh imaa endazhishimod, gaa-piindashkwaanaagwen giiwenh iniw abinoojiinyan, ogashkibidaaganid, miinawaa ko giiwenh gaa-niisiiwesed a'aw abinoojiinh.

paragraph.text_eng: The man said: “I'll kill that evil old woman for sure one of these days. I won’t leave her alone.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh gaa-ikidod a'aw inini, "Booch igo ingoding niwii-niiwana'waa a'aw mindimooyenyish.
Gaawiin indaa-boonenimaasiin," ikido giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: Not long after that old lady was found slumped over. It is said that the dogs chewed at her. The old lady must have been killed as there were marks on her throat. It is said that something must have attacked her.

sentence.sent_text: Wayiiba dash iidog igo wiin gii-mikawind, mii a'aw mindimooyenh, bimi-abid.
Animoshan ogii-kiikamigoon, ikidom giiwenh.
Ogondashkwaang giiwenh gii-eyenizi, gii-niiwana'waawinden a'aw mindimooyenh.
Maagizhaa gaye awiiya gaa-kiikamigogwen, ikidom.

paragraph.text_eng: Even to this day, the old lady’s presence is known to chase people around. She is identified by those shoes.

sentence.sent_text: Noomaya-sh igo geyaabi, ayamanisodawaa giiwenh a'aw mindimooyenh babiminizha'iged.
Mii giiwenh iniw makizinensan gaa-onji-gikenimind.

paragraph.text_eng: It was there where the school is today. There were a lot of graves where the school was, where the school was put, the Indian school. She goes out chasing from there, so nobody can go there. The workers there, the Indians, those that work there at night as custodians, they hear someone breathing hard. One worker quit and another one tried to work. But he told the same CH about sleeping there, that he heard someone breathing hard. So he stopped working there where there were a lot of graves.

sentence.sent_text: Miish imaa noongom gikinoo'amaadiiwigamig imaa gii-tagon.
Gichi-niibowa imaa jiibegamigoon gii-atewan, miish imaa gikinoo'amaadiiwigamig gii-achigaadeg, anishinaabe-gikinoo'amaadiiwigamig.
Miish imaa, mii imaa gaa-onjinizha'iged iko, gaawiin imaa awiiya daa-gii-izhaasiin.
Miish giiwenh ingiw enokiijig imaa, iniw anishinaabeg, imaa niibaadibik ezhi-anokiiwaad, boodawewininiiwiwaad, mii ko ezhi-noondawaawaad gechi-bagidanaamonijin.
Mii gaa-izhi-aanizhiitang imaa a'aw gaa-anokiid bezhig miinawaa bezhig aano-gii-anokii.
Mii go gaye wiin naasaab enaajimod imaa nibaad noondawaad awiiya gichi-bagidanaamonid.
Mii go gaye wiin gaa-izhi-ishkwaa-anokiid imaa, imaa jiibegamigoon gii-paatayiinadoon.

paragraph.text_eng: What I heard long ago about how the white men named Onamia. My late grandmother said it is “Anami’aa” ‘he prays’. She said that a long time ago there were Indians paddling along there. They are going downstream as the river flows, a long way. Long ago it was a big river there where they are paddling.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha giiwenh gaa-izhi-noondamaan i'iw Onamia izhi-wiindamowaad gichi-mookomaanag.
"Anami'aa," gii-ikido ko imaa nookomisiban.
Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod, mewinzha giiwenh imaa bimishkaawaad anishinaabeg.
Iwidi akeyaa niisaaboonowag iwidi iidog akeyaa izhijiwan, waasa i'iw ziibi.
Gii-michaamagad mewinzha gichi-ziibi imaa, imaa bimishkaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Suddenly the canoe comes to a halt. The old man and his party take a look, and behold, the canoe is suspended motionless. It won’t move.

sentence.sent_text: Baanimaa giiwenh ingoding wenji-nagaashkaanig i'iw jiimaan, nagaashkaanig i'iw jiimaan.
Miish giiwenh, inaabiwaad giiwenh imaa a'aw akiwenzii, a'aw akiwenzii imaa, wegwaagi giiwenh ezhi-wenda-gichiwishkaanig i'iw jiimaan.
Mii go gaawiin wii-maajiishkaasinini.

paragraph.text_eng: Behold, there are things that look like huge catfish. One is small. They have horns. And then: “Hey!”; the old man throws tobacco there and speaks of his visions and talks of the manitous as they are afraid that their canoe is sinking.

sentence.sent_text: Wegwaagi giiwenh, indigo giiwenh gichi-owaazisiin ezhinaagozinid.
Bezhig giiwenh agaashiinyiwan.
Odeshkanaawan.

Miish giiwen i'iw, "He," asemaan apaginaawaad imaa miinawaa-sh iidog ezhi-gaagiigidod iniw obawaajigewinan a'aw akiwenzii dazhimaad miinawaa go iniw manidoon, gotamowaad ojiimaaniwaa ji-gondaashkaanig.

paragraph.text_eng: Then their canoe started moving. They wondered what sort of things they had met up with. They look like giant fish with horns, perhaps giant catfish. They used to say that they were some sort of manitou. That’s what they said long ago. That’s why where they prayed [gii-anami’aawaad] is called Onamia.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding igo giiwenh gaa-izhi-maajiishkaanig i'iw ojiimaaniwaa.
Mii iniw gaa-nagishkawaawaajin awegwenan dinowan.
Gichi-giigoonyag izhinaagoziwan odeshkanaawan, maagizhaa gaye gichi-owaazisiin.
"Awegwen manidoo," gii-ikidowag iko.
Mii i'iw gaa-ikidowaad mewinzha.
Miish i'iw wenji-izhi-wiindeg gii-anami'aawaad imaa Onamia.

paragraph.text_eng: Long, long, ago there was an island at Onamia that floated around.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig giiwenh imaa gibaakwa'iganing ayi'ii ko imaa minis gii-pabaamaaboodemagad, gichi-mewinzha go.

paragraph.text_eng: Once there were two men, old men, perhaps they were brothers-in-law, sitting there. They were really feeling good, maybe they had been drinking. It happened a long, long time ago.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingoding niizh ininiwag, akiwenziiyag, maagizhaa gaye gaa-wiitaawigwen, imaa namadabiwaad.
Enda-minwamanji'owag, maagizhaa gaye gaa-minikwewaagwen.
Gichi-mewinzha go gii-aawan.

paragraph.text_eng: Then they must have woken up. That island was right near there.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh, ingoding giiwenh miinawaa dash igo imaa, maagizhaa gaye gaa-koshkoziwaagwen.
Mii giiwenh imaa baa-ayaanig jiigayi'ii i'iw minis.

paragraph.text_eng: “Tayaa,” says one. “Tayaa, let’s go inland. Let’s peel some basswood bark and tie the island down,” he says, so they went inland and peeled some bark. There’s a lot of basswood bark there. They tied up the island there. It didn’t start to float off again. That’s where it remains today. Now it is right next to the land there. There’s not an island there any more. Those old men tied up the island.

sentence.sent_text: "Tayaa," ikido dash giiwenh a'aw.
"Tayaa, daga gopiidaa.
Omaa wiigob bisha'andaa, gitaakwapidoodaa i'iw minis," ikido giiwenh, gaa-izhi-gopiiwaad, gaa-o-izhi-bisha'igobiiwaad.
Niibowa go wiigob imaa.
Miish imaa gaa-izhi-dakobidoowaad i'iw minis.
Mii gaawiin miinawaa gii-maadaaboodesinoon.
Miish igo imaa gii-ayayaag noongom.
Miish igo noongom imaa jiigayi'ii go imaa akiing ezhi-ayaamagak.
Gaawiin geyaabi minisiwanzinoon.
Mii gii-takobidoowaad ingiw akiwenziiyag i'iw minis.

paragraph.text_eng: More of what my late grandmother used to tell me sometimes when she told me stories. Nobody should go across, should go over to that island that is in Mille Lacs Lake. No one should go over there. If someone goes over there, it gets very windy. There is four days of wind if someone goes there.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaa-inaajimod a'aw nookomisiban iko aangodinong dadibaajimotawid.
Gaawiin giiwenh awiiya daa-aazhogesiin imaa, daa-izhaasiin iwidi i'iw minis ayi'ii imaa ayaamagad, minis imaa misi-zaaga'iganiing ayaamagad.
Gaawiin imaa awiiya daa-izhaasiin.
Giishpin awiiya izhaad iwidi, mii ezhi-gichi-noodininig.
Niiyogon-sh giiwenh noodin imaa, giishpin awiiya imaa izhaad.

paragraph.text_eng: She said: “Over there towards the east, from where the sun rises,” she says,” there is a rock there. It’s like it’s flat. That rock is very big,” she says. “Some women were seen there sunning themselves.” I don’t know what they call those women. “They have fishtails,” she says. That’s where those women must have been.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod: "A'aw iwidi akeyaa biidaabang, wenji-biidaabang," ikido, "aya'aa iidog imaa asin.
Mii go ezhi-ayaad, gichi-desaabikizi.
Gichi-mindido a'aw asin," ikido.
"Mii iidog imaa gii-waabamindwaa ingiw ikwewag, abaasandekewaad."
Amanj ezhinikaazowaagwen aya'aag ikwewag.
"Giigoonh-ozhigwanaawag," ikido.
Mii imaa iidog gii-ayaawaad ingiw ikwewag.

paragraph.text_eng: They tell of a big fish there in Mille Lacs Lake. Now the white people are seeing it. Lots of times we see in the papers that they’re seeing a big fish.

sentence.sent_text: Gichi-giigoonh imaa danaajimaa misi-zaaga'iganiing ayaad.
Mii azhigwa waawaabamaawaad ingiw gichi-mookomaanag.
Mazina'iganing igo moozhag niwaabandaamin waabamaawaad iniw gichi-giigoonyan.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago the Indians used to say that they saw it. It’s a very big fish. I don’t know what kind of fish. He said that it is there at the small island off the point. The Indians of old used to say that that’s where it comes from. There is an island there. A whiteman called Minisiiwinini ‘Island-man’ lived there on the small island long ago. That old man was there, he and his family lived there while the Sioux were making war.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha-sh iko gii-ikidowag anishinaabeg gii-waabamaawaad iidog.
Gichi-mindido a'aw gichi-giigoonh.
Awegwen dino giigoonh.
Miish imaa gaa-ikidod mii imaa minisensing ayaad imaa neyaashiing.
Mii imaa wenjiid ikidowag iko gichi-anishinaabeg.
Minis imaa ayaamagad.
Gii-taa ko imaa gichi-mookomaan mewinzha -- Minisiiwinini gii-inaa -- imaa minising.
Mii go megwaa ko bwaanag gii-miigaadiwaad, mii imaa gii-ayaad a'aw akiwenzii, gii-taawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: They say that right in the middle of it is a meadow. It must sink down right there in the middle of it. They say there’s a quaking bog there right in the middle of the island. Nearby is a small rock island. They say that’s where the big fish is. Sometimes when there is a great thunderstorm, he is seen. He runs there to Minisaabikong (Spirit Island), the rock island further on, that’s where he runs to. They say that the water ripples as if there is something under it, that’s how big the fish is.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw imaa naawayi'ii ikidowag, bapashkwaa ikidowag.

Mii go ezhi-dootoobang imaa ikidowag, mii imaa naawayi'ii minising.
Miish imaa besho minisaabikoons ezhi-ayaamagak.
