Mii iwidi epa'iwed minisaabikong; gomaapii go dagon minisaabik, mii iwidi epa'iwed.
Mii go ezhi-oskwaadigoshing ikidowag, eniginid a'aw gichi-giigoonh.

paragraph.text_eng: The rock island is where the lightning bolts always strike, but they're unable to do it -- - I don’t know who those manitous are, Thunderers -- - to kill the big fish.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwidi minisaabikong, miish iidog imaa apane inaabiwin enaabiigiseg, mii go gaye bwaanawi'aawaad ingiw -- - awegwenag ingiw manidoog, animikiig, -- ji-nisaawaapan, mii iniw gichi-giigoonyan.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago the Indians used to see it all the time when it was going to storm. It must be around somewhere in the lake. When it is going to storm, that’s when they see such a high wake going by in the water, as he runs to the rock island, so he said long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Moozhag-sh ko mewinzha ogii-waabamaawaan ingiw anishinaabeg wii-kichi-nichiiwak.
Maagizhaa gaye bebaa-ayaagwen ingoji imaa zaaga'iganiing.
Mii giiwenh wii-kichi-nichiiwak, mii i'iw ezhi-waabandamowaad gomaa go bimi-apiitakidenig i'iw nibi, mii iwidi epa'iwed minisaabikong gii-ikido ko mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: The old men used to tell long ago that a great tunnel runs out from back in the woods, that’s the way the great tunnel must go, out there into the bay where the channel is. Nobody can determine how deep it is. That’s what the Indians always said long ago when it was thundering. There must be a whirlpool there when there is a great thunderstorm. That’s the direction the big tunnel goes.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa-sh iidog mewinzha imaa akeyaa noopiming, ingiw akiwenziiyag iko gii-tibaajimowag, mii imaa wendaayaag gichi-waazh, iidog, miish iwidi akeyaa waasa go owidi akeyaa eni-ayizhi-ayaagwen gichi-waazh, imaa-sh ayi'ing wiikwegamaansing wabibiiyaamagad.
Gaawiin awiiya daa-debakii'igesiin ekwiindimaag.
Mii imaa apane ikidowaad ingiw anishinaabeg mewinzha animikiikaanig.
Mii iidog imaa ezhi-maajijiwang, imaa ezhi-maajijiwang gichi-animikiikaag.
Mii imaa akeyaa ezhi-ayaag i'iw gichi-waazh.

paragraph.text_eng: The Indian used to say all sorts of things long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha go anooj gegoo gii-ikidowag ingiw anishinaabeg.

paragraph.text_eng: And again I used to hear the Indians talking. Long ago they used to be along the shore. The Indians lived there.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa-sh ingiw anishinaabeg ko ninoondawaag gaagiigidowaad.
Miinawaa-sh jiigibiig iko gii-ayaawag mewinzha.
Gii-taawag ingiw anishinaabeg imaa.

paragraph.text_eng: They say that when there is a big thunderstorm, or sometimes when there is a big thunderstorm at night, they would look at the water. The water goes by in a big swell, rising up a great distance, as there’s something speeding by there. That’s where the lightning always strikes, always straight at the island.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iko gichi-animikiikaag, ikidowag, niibaadibik igaye ayaangodinong gichi-animikiikaanig, miish ezhi-waabandamowaad i'iw iidog nibi.
Gomaa giiwenh bimi-apiitakideni, gichi-waasa go apiitakideni, gegoo gichi-bimibidenig iwidi.
Miish imaa giiwenh i'iw inaabiwin imaa enaabiigisenig apane, apane ko giiwenh iwidi gwayak minisaabikong.

paragraph.text_eng: There’s a big fish there, they keep saying, there’s a big fish in Mille Lacs Lake. Now the whitemen are seeing a big fish.

sentence.sent_text: Ayaa-sh igo giiwenh imaa gichi-giigoonh, ikidowag iko, ayaa giiwenh imaa gichi-giigoonh misi-zaaga'iganiing.
Miish azhigwa ingiw gichi-mookomaanag waawaabamaawaad iniw gichi-giigoonyan

paragraph.text_eng: There really must be a big fish in Mille Lacs Lake.

sentence.sent_text: Geget igo ayaa imaa gichi-giigoonh misi-zaaga'iganiing, iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago what the old lady told me about. Maybe they were ricing there towards Beke-zaagidawaag. The road didn’t used to go straight through there where the highway goes. They used to go around Bay Lake. There -- what can I call that lake, maybe it’s called Menisiwang (Farm Island Lake). That lake is really nice.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha gaye a'aw mindimooyenh gaa-inaajimotawid iko.
Maagizhaa gaye gaa-manoominikewaagwen imaa beke-zaagidawaag akeyaa.
Gaawiin-sh iko imaa miikana gii-inamosinoon izhi-gwayak, enamog gichi-miikana iwidi akeyaa.
Mii gaa-izhi-waawaaninishkaawaad zezabegamaag.
Miish imaa -- aaniindanaa ge-izhi-izhinikaadamaambaan i'iw zaaga'igan, menisiwang maagizhaa gaye ezhi-wiindegwen.
Enda-onizhishin sa go i'iw zaaga'igan.

paragraph.text_eng: They must have stopped and slept there in the evening. It must have been when they woke up in the morning -- - maybe they were making tea -- a woman, I don’t know who, was going to dip up water for them to make tea, but she ran inland. “Look over there; there’s a cow swimming by,” she says.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog imaa gaa-izhi-nawajiiwaad ini-onaagoshininig, gaa-izhi-nibaawaad imaa.
Miish iidog gweshkoziwaad azhigwa gigizheb -- maagizhaa gaye eniibiishikewaagwen -- awegwen-sh iidog a'aw ikwe o-gwaaba'ang i'iw nibi wii-aniibiishikewaad giiwenh bi-gopiibatood.
"Nashke gosha naa iwidi inaabig; bizhiki iwidi bimaadagaa," ikido giiwenh.

paragraph.text_eng: Behold, there really was a cow swimming by. He was swimming for the island. They said that it was just as if he was shining with little round spots. That cow was swimming for the island. He must have been a water-cow. “Wonder what sort of manitou he was,” they used to say.

sentence.sent_text: Wegwaagi giiwenh geget bizhiki iwidi gii-pimaadagaa.
Mii imaa enaadagaanid minising.
Miish i'iw gaa-ikidowaad, indigo giiwenh i'iw waasaabikizo, indigo giiwenh gegoo wawaawiyeyaani ezhi-waasaabikizonid.
Mii imaa enaadagaanid akeyaa minising iniw bizhikiwan.
Mii iidog a'aw nibii-bizhiki.
"Awegwen iidog dinowa manidoo," gii-ikidowag iko.

paragraph.text_eng: My late grandmother was once told by her mother about what is called Dabasaakweyaag ‘Stunted Woods’ over on Mille Lacs Lake. A lot of Indians were living there.

sentence.sent_text: Mii gaye a'aw nookomisiban, ingoding igo mii iidog omaa a'aw nookomis gaa-omaamaayijin, ogii-wiindamaagoon, iwidi dabasaakweyaag izhi-wiindemagad imaa misi-zaaga'iganiing.
Mii iidog iwidi gichi-niibowa gaa-taawaad anishinaabeg.

paragraph.text_eng: Along toward evening when it’s real nice, the young people ride horseback and have races. Those young people did all sorts of things when they played.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ini-onaagoshig ko enda-gichi-mino-onaagoshin, mii ingiw oshki-aya'aag bimoomigowaad gagwejikanidiwaad.
Akina sa go gegoo gii-izhichigewag odaminowaad ingiw oshki-aya'aag.

paragraph.text_eng: They had gardens too, and pumpkins. Their gardens grow really well. The pumpkins are huge.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog ingoding miinawaa gitigaan ogii-ayaanaawaa, okosimaanan.
Enda-gichi-minochigewag giiwenh.
Gichi-mamaachaaniwan gaye iniw okosimaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: There is one old man sitting still and smoking. “There’s danger, there’s no doubt something is going to happen to us,” he says. “It’s not good when the garden grows too well. You had better drag those pumpkin vines into the water,” the old man says. “Something bad is going to happen to us.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish iidog a'aw akiwenzii bezhig goshkwaawaadabi zagaswaad.
"Baapiniziwaagan, gaawiin ganabaj naa gegoo giwii-izhiwebizimin," ikido giiwenh.
"Gaawiin onizhishinzinoon i'iw gitigaan onzaamiging.
Indawaaj bakobiidaabaadamok iniw okosimaanan," ikido giiwenh a'aw akiwenzii.
"Giwii-maazhi-izhiwebizimin."

paragraph.text_eng: At this time they were scared of the Sioux. It must have been when they were fighting each other. I don’t know what was really happening to them.

sentence.sent_text: I'iw gaye apii ogii-kosaawaan iniw bwaanan.
Mii iidog i'iw apii megwaa go gii-miigaadiwaad.
Amanj sa iidog gaa-izhiwebiziwaagwen.

paragraph.text_eng: Then, on one fine evening, it’s very still. Along toward evening they saw somebody approaching on foot, a long way down the shore. He falls down there. Then he gets up again. He comes a little closer and then falls down again.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh ingoding enda-mino-onaagoshin, enda-anwaatin.
Eni-onaagoshininig ogii-waabamaawaan giiwenh awiiya biidaasamosenid waasa go iwidi jiigibiig.
Mii ko imaa ezhi-bangishininid.
Mii giiwenh miinawaa ezhi-onishkaanid.
Besho go izhaawan miinawaa ezhi-bangishininid.

paragraph.text_eng: “Hey, who is that over there walking this way?” they thought. Long ago if something happens where the Indians are living, they have one person who takes the news around. If anything happens, he goes and seeks other Indians and tells them.

sentence.sent_text: "He, awenen da naa awedi baadaasamosed?"
miish iidog i'iw gaa-inendamowaad.
Mewinzha ko ingoji anishinaabeg daawaad gegoo izhiwebak, mii iidog ezhi-ayaawaad bezhig igo a'aw dibishkoo sa iidog babaamaajimo.
Gegoo ezhiwebadinig miinawaa ezhi-nandone'waad iniw anishinaaben mii iwidi o-dibaajimod.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the Indians were thinking about, so the men and some women start running (to find out)who he is. When they arrive there, behold it’s a whiteman. Long ago there used to be peddlars around. Those whitemen carry goods on their backs. He went around selling pails and all sorts of things. Maybe he was trading around for things. They really took pity on him and took him back home and tried in vain to doctor him up.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog i'iw gaa-inendamowaad ingiw anishinaabeg, maajiiba'idiwaad giiwenh ingiw ininiwag miinawaa go aanind ikwewag, awenenan iniw.
Bagamiba'idiwaad, wegwaagi giiwenh gichi-mookomaanan.
Mewinzha ko babaamadaawewininiwag gii-ayaawag.
Gii-michiwanewag gichi-mookomaanag.
Akikoon anooj igo gegoo ogii-paa-adaawaagen.
Maagizhaa gaye gaa-paa-meshkwadoonigegwen Owenda-zhawenimaawaan gaa-izhi-maajiinaawaad gaa-izhi-giiwewinaawaad aano-mashkikiikaanaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Then the whiteman died. In a little while one of them started to get a cold. Then another one got sick. Then gradually quite of few of them got sick. Of course the Indians don’t know what’s wrong with them. Gradually the Indians in nearly the whole town are sick or dying.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa giiwenh gaa-izhi-nibod mii a'aw gichi-mookomaan.
Wayiiba go giiwenh bezhig gaa-izhi-mizizid.
Mii go miinawaa bezhig gaa-izhi-aakozid.
Eshkam igo, mii go gomaa go minik aakoziwag.
Aaniish naa gaawiin ogikendanziinaawaa aaniin enaapinewaad ingiw anishinaabeg.
Eshkam igo azhigwa nibowag, eshkam igo mii go gegaa go enigokwaag i'iw anishinaabe-oodena ezhi-aakoziwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: There’s one man living at the end of the village, just older than a young man, with two children and his puppy. There is a big meadow over there. He told his wife that they should move to the woods across the clearing. “Maybe nothing will happen to me,” he thought, so they went there and built a place to stay. Every once in a while they heard shots, gun shots.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig iidog iwidi inini ishkwege, nawaj igo oshki-inini, oniijaanisensan-sh iidog niizhiwan miinawaa odayensan.
Gichi-mashkosiw-sh iwidi ayaamagad, gichi-mashkosiw-sh iwidi ayaamagad iwidi.
Mii iidog gaa-izhi-inaad iniw wiiwan ji-izhi-goziwaad agaamaakwaa.
"Maagizhaa gaawiin gegoo indaa-izhiwebizisiin," gii-inendam, gaa-izhi-maajaawaad gii-o-ozhigewaad, ayayaawaad.
Enda-wewayiiba giiwenh madwewewan, madwewe baashkizigan.

paragraph.text_eng: When anyone dies, there are either three shots or a single shot. It is three shots for an adult. It is a single shot for a child. That’s what the Indians used to do, shoot off guns if anyone dies.

sentence.sent_text: Mii nibod awiiya ayaangoding nising miinawaa aabiding.
Mii nising madweweg mii a'aw gichi-aya'aa.
Aabiding-sh madwewed, mii a'aw abinoojiinh.
Mii ko gaa-izhichigewaad ingiw anishinaabeg, madwezigewaad, nibod awiiya.

paragraph.text_eng: They were living there, when, one morning a while after they woke up, a puppy came running towards them. Behold, it was his puppy, and it fell down there in the doorway, and the man looked at that sick dog of theirs. Then they too started getting sick. The puppy had carried the smallpox there.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding igo giiwenh ayayaawaad, ingoding igo giiwenh gigizheb goshkoziwaad, baanimaa go giiwenh gaa-piijibatood animoons.
Wegwaagi giiwenh iniw odayensan indigo giiwenh gaa-apangishininid imaa ishkwaandeming, aakozinid iniw odayiwaan, ganawaabamaad giiwenh a'aw inini.
Mii sa gaye wiinawaa gaa-izhi-maajinewaad.
Mii iidog a'aw animoons gaa-izhiwidood iwidi i'iw mamakiziwin.

paragraph.text_eng: This certainly happened. Where they lived, the trees don’t grow up. Today it’s called Gaa-dabasaakweyaag ‘Stunted Woods’. The oaks are really short there. That happened for sure.

sentence.sent_text: Geget igo gii-aawan o'o.
Imaa gii-ayaawaad, mii go gaye gaawiin gii-maajiigisiiwag ingiw mitigoog.
Noongom idash gaa-dabasaakweyaag izhi-wiinde.
Ingiw mitigominzhiig enda-dadaakwaakoziwag iwidi.
Geget gii-izhiwebad i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: What the old lady used to tell about the Indians gathering potatoes long ago. After the middle of the summer, the women would travel in a group. They go to the Mississippi River. It was there that the wild potatoes were. Perhaps they slept there while gathering the potatoes. When they get them, they peel some of the potatoes and dry them. They roast some in the coals while they are engaged in picking the potatoes. They get them from the wet places; they got the potatoes from the wet places.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenh giiwenh ingiw anishinaabeg, mii iniw opiniin gii-maamiginaawaad.
Mii gaa-ishkwaa-aabita-niibininig, mii ezhi-maadaawanidiwaad ingiw ikwewag.
Mii iwidi gichi-ziibiing ezhaawaad.
Miish iwidi, mii giiwenh iwidi gii-ayaawaad ingiw bagwaji-opiniig.
Maagizhaa gaye nebaawaagwen iwidi, maamiginaawaad iniw opiniin.
Miish ezhi-ayaawaawaad, aanind ezhi-bishagikonaawaad, baaswaawaad iniw opiniin.
Miinawaa aanind oningwa'abwenaawaan, imaa epiichitaawaad maamiginaawaad iniw opiniin.
Nibiikaang odoondinaawaan, nibiikaang ogii-ondinaawaan iniw opiniin.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady also used to say that the children accompanying them are not to hit each other with the potatoes. No one should be hit by wild potatoes. She used to say that if someone is hit by wild potatoes, he won't live a year. If an Indian is hit by wild potatoes, he dies. That’s what the old lady used to say.

sentence.sent_text: Miish miinawaa, miish iko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenyiban, abinoojiinyan wiijiiwaawaad ji-bakite'odisigwaa iniw opiniin.
Gaawiin giiwenh awiiya daa-bakite'waasiin iniw bagwaji-opiniin.
Mii ko gaa-ikidod a'aw, mii giiwenh giishpin awiiya bakite'ond iniw opiniin, gaawiin ingo-gikinoonowin bimaadizisiin.
Mii giiwenh ezhi-nibod, giishpin bakite'ond iniw opiniin a'aw anishinaabe.
Mii ko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.

paragraph.text_eng: They bring the potatoes back. Then in the winter, having dried all of them, in the winter, the Indians get meat from somewhere. They cook the meat there. They boil the potatoes together with the meat. Then they ate the potatoes.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash giiwenh, mii ezhi-biinaawaad iniw opiniin.
Mii azhigwa bibooninig, akina gii-paaswaawaad, miish bibooninig, ingiw anishinaabeg wiiyaas ingoji ondinamowaad.
Miish imaa wiiyaas gabaatoowaad.
Miish imaa ezhi-dago-onzwaawaad iniw opiniin.
Miish opiniin gii-amwaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago I tried to find out everything. So I asked the old lady: “Where did they get the kettles from, the legged kettles, long ago?”

sentence.sent_text: Gichi-mewinzha akina gegoo ingii-nanda-gikendaan.
Miish iko gaa-izhi-gagwejimag a'aw mindimooyenh: "Aandi gaa-ondinaawaad akikoon mewinzha, okaadakikoon."

paragraph.text_eng: This is what she had to tell about that: “Long ago they were traded for things. They must have traded pelts for the things they wanted a long, long time ago. At one time the legged kettles too must have been given to them. If someone has a legged kettle, she holds on to it always. When an old lady becomes elderly or perhaps is dying, she gives the kettle to her oldest daughter. And so on; that one too, when she becomes an old lady or is dying, might be dying, it is to her daughter that she gives the kettle.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw gaa-inaajimod: "Gichi-mewinzha ko gii-ayaawag gii-meshkwadoonamawindwaa gegoo.
Ayi'ii adaawaagan iidog iko ogii-meshkwadoonaanaawaan gegoo waa-aabajitoowaajin gichi-mewinzha.
Miish iniw okaadakikoon gaye aabiding iidog gaa-izhi-miinindwaa.
Miish igo, giishpin awiiya gaa-ayaawaad iniw okaadakikoon, mii go apane ezhi-ayaawaad.
Mii go gichi-aya'aawid, maagizhaa gaye nibod, mindimooyenh, mii ezhi-miinaad iniw odaanan zeziikizinijin iniw akikoon.
Mii go apane; mii go gaye wiin a'aw mindimooyenyiwid, nibod, maagizhaa gaye nibod, mii go gaye wiin miinawaa iniw odaanan, maanaajin, iniw okaadakikoon."

paragraph.text_eng: “Maybe if the kettle is too heavy, they dig a hole for it somewhere after they boil sap. They use the kettle there again when they parch, when they parch wild rice. If they move camp a long way and can’t carry it along, they just pack it carefully on someone’s back.”

sentence.sent_text: "Maagizhaa gaye onzaam gozigwaninid, mii ezhi-waanikewaad ingoji go ishkwaa-iskigamizigewaad.
Mii gaye imaa aabaji'aawaad iniw akikoon miinawaa go gidasigewaad, manoomin gidasamowaad.
Giishpin idash igo waasa izhi-goziwaad, bwaanawi'aawaad wii-pimiwinaawaad, ogii-wenda-mino'aawaan iniw akikoon bimoomaawaad."

paragraph.text_eng: “If they want to leave it behind somewhere, they dig a hole in the ground. They put the kettle in. In the spring again, they take the kettle to use.”

sentence.sent_text: "Giishpin-sh igo wii-naganaawaad ingoji, mii ezhi-waanikewaad imaa akiing.
Miish imaa biina'waawaad iniw okaadakikoon.
Miinawaa ziigwaninig, miinawaa mamaawaad aabaji'aawaad."

paragraph.text_eng: I asked her: “What sort of thing did they use if they didn’t have a kettle?”

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo gaa-izhi-gagwejimag: "Wegonen dinowa gaa-aabajitoowaad, giishpin gii-ayaawaasigwaa iniw akikoon."

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh,” she says, “over at the Mississippi River,” she said, “there are lots of those ‘iron rushes’, as they call them, along the river,” she says. They weave those plants together. They won’t burn. They weave them carefully so the wild rice won’t fall through. On each side (of the fireplace)they put up sticks, then they put the iron rushes on top. Then the rice is put on top (of them). They build the fire there underneath.

sentence.sent_text: "Oonh," ikido, "gichi-ziibiing iwidi," gii-ikido, "baatayiinadoon iniw biiwaabikwashkoonsan, odizhi-wiindaanan, jiigi-gichi-ziibi baatayiinadoon," ikido.
"Mii gaa-izhi-niibidoowaad, mii iniw mashkosiwan.
Gaawiin daa-jaagidesinoon.
Mii ezhi-niibidoowaad weweni ji-zhaabosesinog i'iw manoomin.
Mii eyiidawayi'ii mitigoon ezhi-badakidoowaad, miish imaa agijayi'ii ezhi-atoowaad, mii iniw biiwaabikwashkoonsan.
Miinawaa i'iw manoomin, mii imaa ezhi-atoowaad agijayi'ii.
Mii iwidi anaamayi'ii ezhi-boodawewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: The iron rushes don’t burn, they just get red-hot,” she said. “They turn it over and over. Then they toast the rice brown.”

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin jaagidesinoon, mii iniw iidog iniw biiwaabikwashkoonsan, mii eta go ezhi-miskwaabikideg," gii-ikido ko.
Mii imaa gwekwekinamowaad.
Miish igo ezhi-ozaawaakizamowaad i'iw manoomin."

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady told about.

sentence.sent_text: Mii imaa gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.

paragraph.text_eng: More of what my grandmother told. It is said that the Indians of long ago had what they called a Throw-Away Moon. It is maybe half-way through the winter, perhaps in the Great Spirit Moon (January).

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaa-inaajimod nookomis.
Mii giiwenh mewinzha ingiw anishinaabeg, miish a'aw webinige-giizis ogii-inaawaan.
Mii iidog i'iw aabita-biboong, maagizhaa gaye gichi-manidoo-giizis.

paragraph.text_eng: It is said that if someone is sick -- - I don’t know where he’d be sick, in his leg or his arm or his back -- then they go and break off a stick.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh awiiya aakozid -- dibi go ji-aakozid, okaading, onikaang, opikwanaang -- mii mitigoons we'o-izhi-bookobidoowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: There at the end they tie tobacco. Then they call out straight up in the sky at the moon. That’s where they throw it. “I throw away my illness,” that’s what they say.

sentence.sent_text: Miish iwidi asemaan ezhi-agwapinaawaad iwidi ishkweyayi'ii.
Mii ezhi-biibaagiwaad, mii iwidi gwayak a'aw giizis agoojing.
Mii iwidi epagidoowaad.
"Niwebinaan indaakoziwin," mii giiwenh ikidowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago the young men were foolish, the boys were foolish.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha giiwenh gii-kagiibaadiziwag oshki-ininiwag, mii go ezhi-gagiibaadiziwaad gwiiwizensag.

paragraph.text_eng: It is after the middle of the winter and the new moon is up. “What shall we throw away” they are saying as they walk around. “Haw, so,”, and they break off sticks and put tobacco there.

sentence.sent_text: Miish giiwenh azhigwa ishkwaa-aabita-bibooninig, oshki-agoojininid iniw giizisoon.
"Wegonesh naa ge-webinamang," ikidowag giiwenh babaamosewaad imaa.
"Haw naa," ezhi-bookobidoowaad giiwenh mitigoons, asemaan asaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: “I throw away my leg,” says one man, one boy. Sure enough, before the year was up, before the middle of the winter came again, he fell and broke his leg. So he lost that leg of his.

sentence.sent_text: "Niwebinaan nikaad," ikido giiwenh bezhig a'aw inini, a'aw gwiiwizens.
Miish giiwenh geget jibwaa-ojijisenig, miinawaa ji-aabita-bibooninig, mii gaa-izhi-bookogaadeshing.
Miish igo gaa-izhi-wanitood i'iw okaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago they used to say “The moon is dying” if the moon gets dark. The Indians were scared when they saw the moon start to get black. Oh, they’re scared, what are they to do?

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha giiwenh, "Nibo a'aw giizis," gii-ikidowag iko, giishpin i'iw ayaad aateyaabikishing.
Gii-segiziwag ingiw anishinaabeg iko iidog gii-waabamaawaad iniw dibik-giizisoon ani-makadewaabikizinid.
Oonh, zegiziwag giiwenh, aaniin ge-izhichigewaad?

paragraph.text_eng: One old man: “Shoot, shoot into the sky!”, he says, and they make an uproar and keep shouting.

sentence.sent_text: Bezhig-sh iidog a'aw akiwenzii: "Mamadwezigeg, ishpiming izhi-mamadwezigeg," ikido giiwenh, gichi-ombiigiziwaad, gichi-baabiibaagiwaad igaye.

paragraph.text_eng: It gets half-dark, sometimes the moon goes almost completely black, and so they keep shooting, hollering, and making lots of noise.

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo azhigwa aabita ani-makadewaabikizinid aangodinong gegaa akina go makadewaabikizinid iniw giizisoon, ezhi-mamadwezigewaad, baabiibaagiwaad, naanoondaagoziwaad igaye.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady used to say: “They revive the moon. Then the blackness of the moon appears to fade away. That’s what they used to say.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish iko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenh: "Odaabaakawi'aawaan iniw giizisoon.
Mii miinawaa ani-izhi-aatenaagozid makadewizid a'aw giizis.
Mii ko gaa-ikidowaad."

paragraph.text_eng: What the Indians did long ago. In the spring when they finish off the sugar, they wouldn’t take a bite of anything unless they first have the necessary feast. They give a feast, have a ceremony, and give thanks for the sugar after they finish it. They finish it just right, as much as they boil from the sap. It’s like that too for wild rice. It’s like that too when they first knock rice.

sentence.sent_text: Ingiw anishinaabeg mewinzha giiwenh gaa-izhichigewaad.
Gaawiin gegoo odaa-gii-izhi-nawadandanziinaawaa, booch igo akawe zagaswe'iwewaad, ziigwaninig, ziinzibaakwad giizhitoowaad.
Mii ezhi-zagaswe'iwewaad, manidookewaad sa go, miigwechiwendamowaad i'iw ziinzibaakwad, giizhitoowaad.
Miish weweni ezhi-giizhitoowaad, minik igo eskigamizigewaad.
Miinawaa i'iw manoomin, mii i'iw gaye dibishkoo.
Mii go gaye dibishkoo, mii go oshki-bawa'amowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: They won't take a bite. Those who have lost a spouse, or maybe if a child of theirs has died, or maybe a relative, must be fed first, spoon-fed. None of the rice would spoil then, or berries, or whatever is ripe. They said that even when the garden is full grown, those people are spoon-fed. They can’t take a bite on their own. They can’t even go swimming in the lake. It’s said of them that the fish go away to avoid them. Those that had lost a spouse were kind of dangerous, and also those who have lost a child.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go gaye gaawiin odaa-izhi-nawadandanziinaawaa.
Miinawaa go ongo zhiigaag, maagizhaa gaye oniijaanisiwaan imaa banaadizinid, maagizhaa gaye odinawemaaganiwaan, mii akawe booch ezhi-ashamindwaa ezhi-zhakamoonda'indwaa i'iw.
Miish gaawiin daa-banaadasinoon i'iw manoomin miinawaa go iniw miinan miinawaa go wegodogwen sa go etiteg.
Gitigaan igo gaye, mii gaa-ikidowaad, mii i'iw giizhigininig mii ezhi-zhakamoonda'indwaa.
Gaawiin odaa-nawadandanziinaawaa.
Booshke go i'iw ayaawaad ji-bagizosigwaa zaaga'iganiing, Mii i'iw gaye gaa-inindwaa, mii i'iw giiwenh giigoonyag ezhi-miidaagwetaawaad.
Gii-aakoodewagiziwag giiwenh ingiw zhiigaag, miinawaa iniw oniijaanisiwaan weni'aawaajin.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady said. She taught me all the things that I wasn’t to do. She taught me everything.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko gaa-ikidod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.
Akina gegoo ingii-kikinoo'amaag ji-izhichigesiwaan.
Akina gegoo ingii-gikinoo'amaag.

paragraph.text_eng: We still do this sometimes. If we get something, rice or sugar or something ripe, then we consider the ones that are mourning. We help them and feed them. Then later on they can eat or pick berries.

sentence.sent_text: Miish igo geyaabi aangodinong ezhichigeyaang.
Giishpin gashkitooyaang gegoo, manoomin igaye miinawaa go ziinzibaakwad miinawaa go iniw etitegin, mii ezhi-mikwenimangidwaa ingiw awiiya gaa-inigaazijig.
Mii ezhi-wiidookawangidwaa ashamangidwaa.
Mii bijiinag ezhi-miijiwaad, mii ezhi-mawinzowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii i'iw.

paragraph.text_eng: What the old lady told me long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw mindimooyenyiban,

paragraph.text_eng: The children long ago said ‘my garden’, when they were children. When they got bigger, they (the parents)sometimes give the one to be married away, arrange an engagement, and go and ask if he or she can marry the girl or boy. Trees somewhere, a tree is selected, two close together. They bend the branches, entwining them. Then when they come of age, they go to see the trees. If one is dried up and withered, they don’t marry each other. If the trees are erect and maturing, then they get married, those of long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog abinoojiinyag mewinzha "ningitigaan" gii-ikidowag, abinoojiinyiwiwaad.
Azhigwa go mamaandidowaad igo, mii iniw ge-wiidigemaajin, aangodinong gii-miigiwewag, gii-miinidiwag, miinawaa gii-nandodamaagewag ji-wiidigemaanid iniw ikwezensan miinawaa gwiiwizensan.
Miish iidog iniw mitigoon ingoji, gaa-izhi-onaabamind a'aw mitig, besho badakizowaad.
Miish iniw ayi'iin, wadikwanan, mii ezhi-onaaginamowaad ezhi-biimaaginamowaad.
Miish azhigwa nitaawigiwaad we'o-izhi-waabamaawaad iniw mitigoon.
Giishpin giiwenh bezhig a'aw baasod bigishkananid, mii gaawiin owiidigemaasiin iniw.
Giishpin-sh giiwenh weweni go badakizowaad maajiigiwaad, mii ezhi-wiidigendiwaad, mii ingiw gichi-mewinzha iidog.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what the old lady told.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko gaa-inaajimod a'aw mindimooyenyiban.

paragraph.text_eng: Again what the old lady told me. She talked about everything with me. It’s long ago and the Indians are cold because the winter is too long. They make bows for the children. They tell them: “Go and shoot up in the sky. Shoot the Wintermaker.” The children go outside and aim skywards. They shoot the Wintermaker. And sure enough it warms up.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw mindimooyenh.
Akina gegoo ingii-waawiindamaag, Mii giiwenh mewinzha anishinaabeg giikajiwaad, onzaam ginwenzh bibooninig.
Mii giiwenh mitigwaabikawaawaad iniw abinoojiinyan.
Miish ezhi-inaawaad: "Ishpiming iwidi o-ina'en.
Bimo gaabiboonoke."
Miish giiwenh ingiw gwiiwizensag zaagiziba'idiwaad, mii iwidi ishpiming ina'ewaad.
Mii iidog bimwaawaad iniw gaabiboonoken.
Miish giiwenh geget ezhi-aabawaag.

paragraph.text_eng: The old lady used to say all kinds of things to me long ago, telling me about things as I was growing up.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko akina gegoo ingii-ig a'aw mindimooyenh gii-waawiindamawid gii-pi-nitaawigiyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what she said of the Indians long ago, that the children are told to settle down as it becomes night. They are not to play around outside. An old lady starts telling stories to them, to the children, preaching to them about everything, and again when they get up in the morning.

sentence.sent_text: Miish i'iw gaa-ikidod gichi-mewinzha giiwenh anishinaabeg, mii go ani-dibikak, mii zagakimindwaa ingiw abinoojiinyag.
Gaawiin agwajiing daa-baa-ayaasiiwag.
Miish a'aw mindimooyenh ezhi-maadaajimotawaad iniw, mii iniw abinoojiinyan, akina gegoo gagiikimaad, miinawaa azhigwa gigizheb goshkoziwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: When a girl can sew, she won’t go out and play around. She is instructed in sewing and they are taught to tan hides. Those are all the things the girls do.

sentence.sent_text: Mii azhigwa nitaa-gashkigwaasod a'aw ikwezens, gaawiin gaye daa-baa-dazhitaasiin.
Mii gikinoo'amawind i'iw ji-gashkigwaadang, ji-gashkigwaasod, miinawaa gikinoo'amawindwaa ji-asekewaad.
Akina go gegoo, mii eta go ezhichigewaad ingiw ikwezensag.

paragraph.text_eng: As for the boys, they were also spoken to this way long ago as they were growing up. When they get bigger, the elders send them out.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go gaye ingiw gwiiwizensag, mii go gaye ingiw gaa-izhi-inindwaa iidog mewinzha, mii azhigwa go eni-nitaawigiwaad.
Ani-mindidowaad, mii i'iw ezhi-maajiinaawaad ingiw gichi-aya'aag.

paragraph.text_eng: “They ‘nandobani’,” she used to say; I don’t know what it meant for them to ‘nandobani’. They taught them how to hunt everything. And the boys fast.

sentence.sent_text: "Nandobaniwag," gii-ikidowag iko; wegodogwen iidog i'iw gii-nandobaniwaad.
Miish giiwenh gaa-izhi-gikinoo'amawaawaad ji-nitaa-giiyosenid akina go gegoo.
Miinawaa gii'igoshimowag ingiw gwiiwizensag.

paragraph.text_eng: The girls fast too. As soon as it gets to be toward spring, the girls are given charcoal when they wake in the morning and they mark themselves. Sometimes they rub the charcoal on their faces. When they think of someone they can go fasting with, they go to one of the wigwams. Before any of them can eat, she takes the charcoal.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go gaye ikwezensag ezhi-gii'igoshimowaad.
Mii azhigwa ani-ziigwang ingiw ikwezensag, mii ezhi-miinindwaa akakanzhe bi-goshkoziwaad gigizheb, ezhi-beshibii'odizowaad.
Aangodinong igaye imaa odengwaawaang ezhi-zinigonamowaad akakanzhe.
Mii ezhi-maajaawaad bezhig igo wiigiwaam, awiiya mikwenimaawaad ge-wiiji-gii'igoshimomaawaajin.
Mii miinawaa awiiya jibwaa-wiisinid, mii i'iw akakanzhe ezhi-mamood.
Aangodinong niizhogon gaawiin wiisinisiiwag, mii gaa-izhi'indwaa mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: They are taught to make an abwaanaak ‘roasting frame’ when someone kills game. They cut the meat up into strips. They hang it up there. The only way they were able to preserve the meat was to process it over the fire. If they had a lot of meat, all kinds of it, then they make an agoojiwanaanaak ‘hanging frame’ and hang it up there. They put the meat away in birchbark baskets. This is so the dogs or animals or anything can’t get at it. These are called agoojiwanaanaakoon ‘hanging frames’.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa mii ezhi-gikinoo'amawindwaa awiiya nitaaged, mii ezhi-ozhitoowaad abwaanaak.
Miish i'iw wiiyaas ezhi-baanizhamowaad.
Mii imaa ezhi-agoodoowaad.
Mii eta akeyaa gaa-izhi-gashkitoowaad i'iw wiiyaas gii-kanawendamowaad abwaadamowaad i'iw wiiyaas.
Miinawaa niibowa ayaamowaad wiiyaas anooj igo gegoo, mii ezhi-ozhitoowaad agoojiwanaanaak, iwidi agoodoowaad.
Wiigwaasi-makakong obiina'aanaawaa i'iw wiiyaas.
Miish ingiw animoshag, maagizhaa gaye awesiinyag, anooj igo awiiya ji-debandanzig.
Agoojiwanaanaakoon gii-izhi-wiindewan.

paragraph.text_eng: In the summer they pick berries, all kinds of berries, chokecherries, blueberries, anything that is ripe. They dry them. They put them away in birchbark baskets. They get what they have for tea from the swamps. If anyone wanted to be lazy, he’d starve. They won’t help each other out very much.

sentence.sent_text: Mii miinawaa niibininig ezhi-mawinzowaad, anooj igo gegoo asasaweminan, miinan, akina sa go gegoo etitenig.
Mii ezhi-baasamowaad.
Miish ezhi-biina'amowaad imaa wiigwaasi-makakong.
Miish i'iw miinawaa go wedaniibiishimiwaad, waabashkikiing ogii-ondinaanaawaa.
Mii go awiiya wii-pagandizid, mii i'iw ezhi-gawanaandang iidog.
Gaawiin ge-wiidookodaadisiiwag aapiji sa go.

paragraph.text_eng: They go away, sometimes to the Mississippi, taking the children along to pick those wild potatoes. Sometimes they take the children along. The children are not supposed to go and hit each other with the potatoes. If they hit each other with potatoes, then before one year is up the one that is hit with potatoes dies, so they are forbidden to go around hitting one another with the potatoes.

sentence.sent_text: Mii miinawaa ezhi-maajaawaad, aangodinong iwidi gichi-ziibiing izhaawag, wiijiiwaawaad iniw abinoojiinyan, o-maamiginaawaad iniw aya'aan bagwaji-opiniin.
Aangodinong gaye abinoojiinyan ogii-wiijiiwaawaan.
Miish giiwenh gaawiin ingiw abinoojiinyag daa-o-bapakite'odisiiwag iniw opiniin.
Giishpin bakite'odiwaad iniw opiniin, mii go giiwenh jibwaa-ningo-gikinoonowagak ezhi-nibod wa'aw bekite'ond iniw opiniin, ezhi-gina'amawindwaa ji-baa-bapakite'odisigwaa iniw opiniin.

paragraph.text_eng: They did everything to survive long ago. The girls just sit on their knees and sew. They wouldn’t wander around any place.

sentence.sent_text: Akina go gegoo gii-izhichigewag, gaa-onji-bimaadiziwaad mewinzha.
Mii eta go bidigwesabiwaad gashkigwaasowaad ingiw ikwezensag.
Gaawiin igaye ingoji daa-baa-ayaasiiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: More of what my late grandmother told. Those that lived in different places were related by sharing a totem, that’s how they were related. I don’t know what she told of that.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa-sh i'iw nookomisiban gaa-inaajimod.
Mii giiwenh gaa-izhi-inawendiwaad, gaa-ayindaawaad ezhi-odoodemiwaad mii akeyaa gaa-izhi-ayinawendiwaad.
Amanj-sh iidog gaa-inaajimogwen.

paragraph.text_eng: Some of the Indians came from the north and some were at Madeline Island along the shore of Lake Superior. They lived in groups according to their relationship.

sentence.sent_text: Aanind iwidi akeyaa giiwedinong gii-onjibaawag ingiw anishinaabeg miinawaa iwidi aanind mooningwanekaaning gii-ayaawag zhizhodewe-gichigami.
Mii sa go ezhi-ayinawendiwaad gaa-izhi-wawiko-ayaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Another thing she told me was that there was a big war, perhaps with the Sioux. The Martens were very foolish. They lived under the ground. They are called earthen lodges. That’s the kind of place the Martens lived in. The Sioux must have thrown gunpowder in there. They exploded and those called Martens were wiped out. They spared only a girl and a boy, so it used to be said.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa-sh iko gaa-izhi-wiindamawid gii-kichi-miigaadiwag, maagizhaa gaye bwaanag.
Miinawaa-sh ingiw gii-wenda-gagiibaadiziwag giiwenh mii ingiw waabizheshiwag.
Anaamakamig gii-taawag.
Akiiwe-wiigiwaaman gii-izhi-wiindewan.
Mii imaa dinong gii-taawaad ingiw waabizheshiwag.
Miish imaa, miish iidog ingiw bwaanag gaa-izhi-biinjwebinamowaad makade imaa.
Miish imaa gaa-izhi-baashkidenig, miish i'iw gaa-izhi-jaaginanindwaa, mii ingiw aya'aag waabizheshiwag gaa-ininjig.
Mii sa eta ikwezensan miinawaa gwiiwizensan, ogii-ishkonaawaan gii-ikidom iko.

paragraph.text_eng: There are a lot of Martens today. A lot of the Martens are born, a whole lot of them. And the Martens weren’t allowed to marry each other as they were related. They weren’t allowed to -- - I don’t know why they weren’t allowed to. It’s just like they are siblings, like brothers to each other, those Martens.

sentence.sent_text: Noongom idash gichi-baatayiinowag ingiw waabizheshiwag.
Baatayiinowag imaa niigiwaad ingiw waabizheshiwag gichi-baatayiinowag.
Miinawaa gaawiin gii-pagidinaasiiwag ji-izhi-wiidigendiwaad ezhi-inawendiwaad, mii ingiw waabizheshiwag.
Gaawiin gii-pagidinaasiiwag -- amanj i'iw gii-pagidinaasiwindwaa.
Dibishkoo go odawemaawaan, dibishkoo sa go wiijikiwenyindiwaad mii ingiw waabizheshiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s the way my grandmother used to tell it. If one of them marries another Marten, the children don’t grow up straight. That’s what the old lady used to tell me.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ko akeyaa gaa-inaajimod a'aw nookomisiban.
Giishpin wiidigemaad iniw waabizheshiwan, gaawiin gwayakogisiiwan oniijaanisiwaan.
Mii ko gaa-inaajimotawid a'aw nookomisiban.
